PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST AND HOLD CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE.
California’s community health clinics receive billions of taxpayer dollars to provide care for people who need it most. Yet some clinics spend less than half of their funding on patient care and services, while large portions of their revenue go to bloated CEO salaries and other wasteful spending. As a result, patients wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with staffing shortages, outdated equipment, and limited resources.
WHY PROP. 44 IS NEEDED
Community health clinics receive taxpayer funding for one purpose: to provide primary care, mental health services, dental care, prenatal care, vaccinations, and other essential services to millions of children, seniors, working families, and Californians with disabilities. Without access to these clinics, many patients would not get the care they urgently need. But some clinic CEOs are misusing taxpayer dollars by diverting millions to inflated executive salaries and other non-essentials.
With massive federal healthcare cuts expected to eliminate billions in funding for California’s healthcare system, community clinics will be among the hardest hit. Clinics may be forced to reduce services, lay off staff, or even close their doors. That means every healthcare dollar matters more than ever. California taxpayers can’t afford to waste resources that should be helping patients receive timely, high-quality care.
PROP. 44 DIRECTS HEALTHCARE DOLLARS TO PATIENT CARE
Proposition 44 is simple. It requires community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on their non-profit mission-patient care and the services that make care possible. That could include medical visits, mental health care, dental care, medications, medical equipment, transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, outreach, and other services that serve the clinics’ charitable healthcare mission.
What doesn’t count towards the 90%: excessive CEO pay, lavish events, bloated overhead, and other spending that takes resources away from the clinic’s core mission of caring for patients.
PROP. 44 HOLDS CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE
Proposition 44 will increase transparency by requiring clinics to publicly report how healthcare dollars are spent, so patients and taxpayers can hold them accountable. Currently, there are hundreds of millions of dollars in the clinic system that are not being spent on the core mission of patient care. Prop. 44 will make sure those healthcare dollars go where they can do the most good.
This measure does not cut clinic funding or reduce services patients rely on. Clinics that meet the standard keep every dollar, and even clinics that fall short can recover any penalties by coming into compliance. Unrecovered penalties, if any, are redirected to recruiting, training, and retaining the healthcare workers our clinics desperately need. Every dollar stays in the healthcare system-prioritized for patient care instead of excessive overhead.
Join healthcare workers, patients, and Californians who believe accountability strengthens our healthcare system.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST.
Shawna Brown , Initiative Proponent
Brisa J. Barrera , Community Clinic Worker
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
PROP. 44 IS A DANGEROUS SPECIAL INTEREST MEASURE THAT THREATENS CARE FOR MILLIONS
Make no mistake: Prop. 44 is not about resources for patient care. Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure written and funded entirely by one special interest that threatens access to care for millions. Prop. 44 imposes unworkable restrictions that actually prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need.
NURSES, DOCTORS AND PATIENT ADVOCATES ALL AGREE: PROP. 44 WILL HURT PATIENTS. Prop. 44 will:
• Cut billions from health clinics every year. • Force clinics to shut down and cut services. • Eliminate care for millions. • Send more patients to hospital ERs-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 IS UNNECESSARY. COMMUNITY CLINICS ARE STRICTLY REGULATED.
Community clinics are heavily regulated, with strict rules requiring resources be spent on patient care and serving their communities. Federal and state laws require regular audits and public reporting of clinic spending. Every community clinic is not-for-profit-led by a board that includes patients-requiring funds to be spent on patient care and community benefits-not corporate profits.
SPECIAL INTERESTS PUSHING PROP. 44 ARE USING PATIENTS AS PAWNS
Prop. 44 is a shameful power play by one special interest abusing the ballot measure process to gain political leverage over health clinics. This same special interest has spent $140 million pushing dozens of harmful ballot measures against hospitals, clinics and physicians, including three unsuccessful dialysis propositions that voters overwhelmingly rejected.
JOIN PATIENTS, NURSES, DOCTORS, AND COMMUNITY LEADERS: NO ON PROP. 44.
Prop. 44 is opposed by:
• American Academy of Pediatrics CA • California School Nurses Organization • California Medical Association • American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists District IX • Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA • American College of Emergency Physicians CA • California Academy of Family Physicians
www.NoProp44.com
Brent K Sugimoto , MD, FAAFP, President-Elect
California Academy of Family Physicians
Kelly McCue , MD, Immediate Past Chair
American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists District IX
Susanne J. Spano , MD, FACEP, President
American College of Emergency Physicians, California Chapter
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 44
VOTE NO ON PROP. 44: STOP THE ATTACK ON PATIENTS & COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS
Prop. 44 is a dangerous, poorly drafted measure that would threaten care for millions of California patients.
Prop. 44 imposes deeply flawed and unworkable restrictions that prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need. Economic and health experts warn Prop. 44 will:
• Cut $1.7 billion from health clinics in the first year alone. • Cause 88% of all clinics in the state to operate at a loss. • Force thousands of clinics throughout the state to cut back patient services or shut down entirely. • Eliminate care for millions of Californians. • Send more patients to hospital emergency rooms-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 ARBITRARILY RESTRICTS SPENDING ON VITAL PATIENT SERVICES
Prop. 44 is so poorly written that it restricts clinics from spending resources on essential staff and services, including nurse managers, physician leaders, translation services, insurance assistance and community education. It even restricts clinics from funding mammogram, X-ray and CT machines, information technology and expanding or upgrading clinics.
PROP. 44 DECIMATES THE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM AND HURTS ALL PATIENTS
Community health clinics provide primary care, prenatal care, urgent care, mental and behavioral health services, telehealth, and dental services. They operate school-based health clinics that care for hundreds of thousands of children.
Community clinics serve 1 in 4 Medi-Cal patients, the uninsured, working families, seniors, veterans, and children. In many rural and medically underserved communities, community health clinics are the only source of care within hundreds of miles.
Prop. 44 will make our bad healthcare problems even worse- increasing patient wait times and eliminating the only source of care for many patients.
PROP. 44 IS UNNECESSARY. COMMUNITY CLINICS ARE STRICTLY REGULATED.
Community clinics are already heavily regulated by the federal and state governments, with strict funding rules on patient care and essential services, and regular mandatory public audits. All clinics are overseen by patient board members, to ensure care is focused on community needs. And clinics are non-profits legally required to focus resources on patient services and community benefits.
PROP. 44 OPPOSED BY PATIENTS, NURSES, DOCTORS AND COMMUNITY LEADERS
“Prop. 44 will eliminate the only source of care in many communities. Please vote NO.” -Kim Yu, MD, FAAFP, President, California Academy of Family Physicians
“Community clinics are a lifeline for my family and millions across California. Please, protect patients like me. Reject Prop. 44.” -Carmen Huertero, Clinic Patient, San Marcos, CA
“Prop. 44 threatens women’s access to healthcare at a time when it’s already under attack. Vote No.” -Jodi Hicks, President & CEO, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
"By shutting down clinics, Prop. 44 will force millions of patients into already overcrowded emergency rooms-increasing wait times for everyone.” -Susanne J Spano, MD, FACEP, President, American College of Emergency Physicians, California
“Prop. 44 threatens to shut down hundreds of school-based clinics that provide primary care, vaccinations, health screenings and mental health services for tens of thousands of children. Vote NO.” -Katie Nilsson, RN, President, California School Nurses Organization
Prop. 44 Opposed By:
• American Academy of Pediatrics, California • California School Nurses Organization • California Medical Association • California Primary Care Association, representing thousands of community health centers and clinics • American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists District IX • Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California • National Association of Social Workers, California Chapter • American College of Emergency Physicians, California • California Academy of Family Physicians
www.NoProp44.com
Eric Ball , MD, FAAP, President
American Academy of Pediatrics, California
Katie Nilsson , RN, President
California School Nurses Organization
René Bravo , M.D., President
California Medical Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 44
DON’T BE FOOLED BY SCARE TACTICS.
Highly paid clinic executives want you to believe this measure will close clinics, eliminate services, and hurt patients. Those claims are false.
PROP. 44 PROTECTS PATIENT CARE-IT DOESN'T CUT IT.
Proposition 44 simply requires that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ non-profit mission: patient care and services that support care. This CAN INCLUDE: Transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, community outreach, nurse managers and clinical staff, medical equipment and information technology, and mental health, dental, and preventative care. The opposition falsely claims these services would be cut, but Prop. 44 is designed to protect spending that serves patients.
PROP. 44 PREVENTS PRECIOUS RESOURCES FROM BEING DIVERTED AWAY FROM PATIENT CARE
Prop. 44 seeks to reduce spending on: Excessive CEO pay, lavish events, expensive consultants, and unnecessary administrative spending. That means healthcare dollars would go where they belong: Caring for patients.
WHY ARE CLINIC EXECUTIVES FIGHTING ACCOUNTABILITY?
The campaign against Prop. 44 is funded by the same highly paid clinic executives who benefit from the current system. If today’s oversight were enough, some clinics wouldn’t be spending less than half of their funding on patient care and services. The real threat to clinics isn’t accountability, it’s devastating federal healthcare cuts. Patients can’t afford to see precious funding spent on excessive CEO compensation and other non-essentials while they wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with understaffing and limited resources.
PUT PATIENTS FIRST, NOT CLINIC CEOS.
Vote YES on Proposition 44.
Shawna Brown , Initiative Proponent
Brisa J. Barrera , Community Clinic Worker

The ballot measure proposes a new rule: These clinics would have to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and services tied to their mission.
Right now, they average about 80%.
Miss that target, and the clinic pays a penalty.
They can earn it back if they hit 90% within five years.
If not, the state keeps the money.
Supporters, led by the healthcare union SEIU-UHW, say it stops wasteful spending on executive pay and forces accountability.
Opponents — including both major state parties, Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association — say clinics can’t realistically hit 90%.
One analysis found 89% of California clinic organizations would fail in year one, facing $1.6 billion in fines.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST AND HOLD CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE.
California’s community health clinics receive billions of taxpayer dollars to provide care for people who need it most. Yet some clinics spend less than half of their funding on patient care and services, while large portions of their revenue go to bloated CEO salaries and other wasteful spending. As a result, patients wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with staffing shortages, outdated equipment, and limited resources.
WHY PROP. 44 IS NEEDED
Community health clinics receive taxpayer funding for one purpose: to provide primary care, mental health services, dental care, prenatal care, vaccinations, and other essential services to millions of children, seniors, working families, and Californians with disabilities. Without access to these clinics, many patients would not get the care they urgently need. But some clinic CEOs are misusing taxpayer dollars by diverting millions to inflated executive salaries and other non-essentials.
With massive federal healthcare cuts expected to eliminate billions in funding for California’s healthcare system, community clinics will be among the hardest hit. Clinics may be forced to reduce services, lay off staff, or even close their doors. That means every healthcare dollar matters more than ever. California taxpayers can’t afford to waste resources that should be helping patients receive timely, high-quality care.
PROP. 44 DIRECTS HEALTHCARE DOLLARS TO PATIENT CARE
Proposition 44 is simple. It requires community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on their non-profit mission-patient care and the services that make care possible. That could include medical visits, mental health care, dental care, medications, medical equipment, transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, outreach, and other services that serve the clinics’ charitable healthcare mission.
What doesn’t count towards the 90%: excessive CEO pay, lavish events, bloated overhead, and other spending that takes resources away from the clinic’s core mission of caring for patients.
PROP. 44 HOLDS CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE
Proposition 44 will increase transparency by requiring clinics to publicly report how healthcare dollars are spent, so patients and taxpayers can hold them accountable. Currently, there are hundreds of millions of dollars in the clinic system that are not being spent on the core mission of patient care. Prop. 44 will make sure those healthcare dollars go where they can do the most good.
This measure does not cut clinic funding or reduce services patients rely on. Clinics that meet the standard keep every dollar, and even clinics that fall short can recover any penalties by coming into compliance. Unrecovered penalties, if any, are redirected to recruiting, training, and retaining the healthcare workers our clinics desperately need. Every dollar stays in the healthcare system-prioritized for patient care instead of excessive overhead.
Join healthcare workers, patients, and Californians who believe accountability strengthens our healthcare system.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST.

# Why California Healthcare Workers And Clinic Boards Clash Over Prop. 44
## Labor Unions Endorse Ballot Measure; Physicians, Medical Executives Oppose It
...
- Oct 22, 2026
...
TRI-VALLEY—A statewide union of healthcare workers, patients, and consumers, and the boards of community health clinics, stand on opposite sides of Proposition 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.
Although the legislation's ultimate impact remains unclear, a passing vote would require the California Attorney General to issue binding guidance clarifying two key economic figures for clinics: total revenue and total program spending.
The legislation reached the Nov. 3 general ballot because Service Employees International Union - United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW) gathered 546,651 signatures.
Representing over 120,000 healthcare workers and consumers, the union is backed by the California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO).
Renée Saldaña, press secretary for SEIU-UHW, said due to federal funding cuts enacted through HR 1, California will lose up to $30 billion in health care funding in 2027.
“We started a grassroots effort to counter this massive crisis coming to the state’s healthcare system.
We expect longer waits and fewer services.”
The community clinics affected by the bill are nonprofit organizations called federally qualified health centers (FQHCs).
These centers provide primary, dental, and behavioral health care in California’s medically underserved communities.

44 here, along with the editorial board’s take on the issue.*
There’s a measure on your California ballot that could change spending rules for community health clinics.
Let’s talk Prop.
44.
Proposition 44 targets federally qualified health centers.
Those are the nonprofit clinics that serve underserved communities across California.
There’s about 2,000 of them.
The ballot measure proposes a new rule: These clinics would have to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and services tied to their mission.
Right now, they average about 80%.
Miss that target, and the clinic pays a penalty.
They can earn it back if they hit 90% within five years.
If not, the state keeps the money.
Supporters, led by the healthcare union SEIU-UHW, say it stops wasteful spending on executive pay and forces accountability.
Opponents — including both major state parties, Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association — say clinics can’t realistically hit 90%.
One analysis found 89% of California clinic organizations would fail in year one, facing $1.6 billion in fines.

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST AND HOLD CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE.
California’s community health clinics receive billions of taxpayer dollars to provide care for people who need it most. Yet some clinics spend less than half of their funding on patient care and services, while large portions of their revenue go to bloated CEO salaries and other wasteful spending. As a result, patients wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with staffing shortages, outdated equipment, and limited resources.
WHY PROP. 44 IS NEEDED
Community health clinics receive taxpayer funding for one purpose: to provide primary care, mental health services, dental care, prenatal care, vaccinations, and other essential services to millions of children, seniors, working families, and Californians with disabilities. Without access to these clinics, many patients would not get the care they urgently need. But some clinic CEOs are misusing taxpayer dollars by diverting millions to inflated executive salaries and other non-essentials.
With massive federal healthcare cuts expected to eliminate billions in funding for California’s healthcare system, community clinics will be among the hardest hit. Clinics may be forced to reduce services, lay off staff, or even close their doors. That means every healthcare dollar matters more than ever. California taxpayers can’t afford to waste resources that should be helping patients receive timely, high-quality care.
PROP. 44 DIRECTS HEALTHCARE DOLLARS TO PATIENT CARE
Proposition 44 is simple. It requires community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on their non-profit mission-patient care and the services that make care possible. That could include medical visits, mental health care, dental care, medications, medical equipment, transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, outreach, and other services that serve the clinics’ charitable healthcare mission.
What doesn’t count towards the 90%: excessive CEO pay, lavish events, bloated overhead, and other spending that takes resources away from the clinic’s core mission of caring for patients.
PROP. 44 HOLDS CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE
Proposition 44 will increase transparency by requiring clinics to publicly report how healthcare dollars are spent, so patients and taxpayers can hold them accountable. Currently, there are hundreds of millions of dollars in the clinic system that are not being spent on the core mission of patient care. Prop. 44 will make sure those healthcare dollars go where they can do the most good.
This measure does not cut clinic funding or reduce services patients rely on. Clinics that meet the standard keep every dollar, and even clinics that fall short can recover any penalties by coming into compliance. Unrecovered penalties, if any, are redirected to recruiting, training, and retaining the healthcare workers our clinics desperately need. Every dollar stays in the healthcare system-prioritized for patient care instead of excessive overhead.
Join healthcare workers, patients, and Californians who believe accountability strengthens our healthcare system.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST.
Shawna Brown , Initiative Proponent
Brisa J. Barrera , Community Clinic Worker
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
PROP. 44 IS A DANGEROUS SPECIAL INTEREST MEASURE THAT THREATENS CARE FOR MILLIONS
Make no mistake: Prop. 44 is not about resources for patient care. Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure written and funded entirely by one special interest that threatens access to care for millions. Prop. 44 imposes unworkable restrictions that actually prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need.
NURSES, DOCTORS AND PATIENT ADVOCATES ALL AGREE: PROP. 44 WILL HURT PATIENTS. Prop. 44 will:
• Cut billions from health clinics every year. • Force clinics to shut down and cut services. • Eliminate care for millions. • Send more patients to hospital ERs-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 IS UNNECESSARY. COMMUNITY CLINICS ARE STRICTLY REGULATED.
Community clinics are heavily regulated, with strict rules requiring resources be spent on patient care and serving their communities. Federal and state laws require regular audits and public reporting of clinic spending. Every community clinic is not-for-profit-led by a board that includes patients-requiring funds to be spent on patient care and community benefits-not corporate profits.
SPECIAL INTERESTS PUSHING PROP. 44 ARE USING PATIENTS AS PAWNS
Prop. 44 is a shameful power play by one special interest abusing the ballot measure process to gain political leverage over health clinics. This same special interest has spent $140 million pushing dozens of harmful ballot measures against hospitals, clinics and physicians, including three unsuccessful dialysis propositions that voters overwhelmingly rejected.
JOIN PATIENTS, NURSES, DOCTORS, AND COMMUNITY LEADERS: NO ON PROP. 44.
Prop. 44 is opposed by:
• American Academy of Pediatrics CA • California School Nurses Organization • California Medical Association • American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists District IX • Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA • American College of Emergency Physicians CA • California Academy of Family Physicians

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 44
VOTE NO ON PROP. 44: STOP THE ATTACK ON PATIENTS & COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS
Prop. 44 is a dangerous, poorly drafted measure that would threaten care for millions of California patients.
Prop. 44 imposes deeply flawed and unworkable restrictions that prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need. Economic and health experts warn Prop. 44 will:
• Cut $1.7 billion from health clinics in the first year alone. • Cause 88% of all clinics in the state to operate at a loss. • Force thousands of clinics throughout the state to cut back patient services or shut down entirely. • Eliminate care for millions of Californians. • Send more patients to hospital emergency rooms-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 ARBITRARILY RESTRICTS SPENDING ON VITAL PATIENT SERVICES
Prop. 44 is so poorly written that it restricts clinics from spending resources on essential staff and services, including nurse managers, physician leaders, translation services, insurance assistance and community education. It even restricts clinics from funding mammogram, X-ray and CT machines, information technology and expanding or upgrading clinics.
PROP. 44 DECIMATES THE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM AND HURTS ALL PATIENTS
Community health clinics provide primary care, prenatal care, urgent care, mental and behavioral health services, telehealth, and dental services. They operate school-based health clinics that care for hundreds of thousands of children.
Community clinics serve 1 in 4 Medi-Cal patients, the uninsured, working families, seniors, veterans, and children. In many rural and medically underserved communities, community health clinics are the only source of care within hundreds of miles.
Prop. 44 will make our bad healthcare problems even worse- increasing patient wait times and eliminating the only source of care for many patients.
PROP. 44 IS UNNECESSARY. COMMUNITY CLINICS ARE STRICTLY REGULATED.
Community clinics are already heavily regulated by the federal and state governments, with strict funding rules on patient care and essential services, and regular mandatory public audits. All clinics are overseen by patient board members, to ensure care is focused on community needs. And clinics are non-profits legally required to focus resources on patient services and community benefits.
PROP. 44 OPPOSED BY PATIENTS, NURSES, DOCTORS AND COMMUNITY LEADERS
“Prop. 44 will eliminate the only source of care in many communities. Please vote NO.” -Kim Yu, MD, FAAFP, President, California Academy of Family Physicians

"By shutting down clinics, Prop. 44 will force millions of patients into already overcrowded emergency rooms-increasing wait times for everyone.” -Susanne J Spano, MD, FACEP, President, American College of Emergency Physicians, California
“Prop. 44 threatens to shut down hundreds of school-based clinics that provide primary care, vaccinations, health screenings and mental health services for tens of thousands of children. Vote NO.” -Katie Nilsson, RN, President, California School Nurses Organization

REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 44
DON’T BE FOOLED BY SCARE TACTICS.
Highly paid clinic executives want you to believe this measure will close clinics, eliminate services, and hurt patients. Those claims are false.
PROP. 44 PROTECTS PATIENT CARE-IT DOESN'T CUT IT.
Proposition 44 simply requires that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ non-profit mission: patient care and services that support care. This CAN INCLUDE: Transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, community outreach, nurse managers and clinical staff, medical equipment and information technology, and mental health, dental, and preventative care. The opposition falsely claims these services would be cut, but Prop. 44 is designed to protect spending that serves patients.
PROP. 44 PREVENTS PRECIOUS RESOURCES FROM BEING DIVERTED AWAY FROM PATIENT CARE
Prop. 44 seeks to reduce spending on: Excessive CEO pay, lavish events, expensive consultants, and unnecessary administrative spending. That means healthcare dollars would go where they belong: Caring for patients.
WHY ARE CLINIC EXECUTIVES FIGHTING ACCOUNTABILITY?
The campaign against Prop. 44 is funded by the same highly paid clinic executives who benefit from the current system. If today’s oversight were enough, some clinics wouldn’t be spending less than half of their funding on patient care and services. The real threat to clinics isn’t accountability, it’s devastating federal healthcare cuts. Patients can’t afford to see precious funding spent on excessive CEO compensation and other non-essentials while they wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with understaffing and limited resources.
PUT PATIENTS FIRST, NOT CLINIC CEOS.
Vote YES on Proposition 44.
Shawna Brown , Initiative Proponent
Brisa J. Barrera , Community Clinic Worker

Each covered clinic would have to spend at least 90 percent of its total annual revenue on “program services” that advance its charitable mission, meaning patient care and related services rather than management, overhead, or accumulated surplus [1, Sec. 3].
The measure works through a ratio it calls the mission spend ratio.
That ratio is the amount a clinic spends on activities accomplishing its exempt purpose divided by its total revenue [1, Sec. 3].
The building blocks come from the clinic’s IRS Form 990.
The numerator starts from “total program service expenses” on line 4e of Part III, and the denominator starts from total revenue on line 12 of Part I, for tax year 2024 or later [1, Sec. 3(b)(1)].
The attorney general may issue binding guidance adjusting how both figures are counted, so the final definition of qualifying spending is not fixed in the text—it is delegated [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
A clinic whose mission spend ratio falls below 90 percent would owe an administrative penalty equal to the gap between what it actually spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of its total revenue [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)].

Each covered clinic would have to spend at least 90 percent of its total annual revenue on “program services” that advance its charitable mission, meaning patient care and related services rather than management, overhead, or accumulated surplus [1, Sec. 3].
The measure works through a ratio it calls the mission spend ratio.
That ratio is the amount a clinic spends on activities accomplishing its exempt purpose divided by its total revenue [1, Sec. 3].
The building blocks come from the clinic’s IRS Form 990.
The numerator starts from “total program service expenses” on line 4e of Part III, and the denominator starts from total revenue on line 12 of Part I, for tax year 2024 or later [1, Sec. 3(b)(1)].
The attorney general may issue binding guidance adjusting how both figures are counted, so the final definition of qualifying spending is not fixed in the text—it is delegated [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
A clinic whose mission spend ratio falls below 90 percent would owe an administrative penalty equal to the gap between what it actually spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of its total revenue [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)].

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-dateline data-subscriber-content> SACRAMENTO — The California Primary Care Assn. and five clinics filed a civil lawsuit in federal court Friday accusing SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West and its president, Dave Regan, of racketeering and using ballot initiatives to “shake down” community health centers.
The association alleges that Regan and his union orchestrated a “multi-year campaign of coercion, threats, and economic pressure” to “extort” what the lawsuit describes as “valuable property rights” and “labor-organizing terms” from CPCA and the health centers the association represents in California, according to a copy of the complaint obtained by The Times.
The suit says Regan pushed Proposition 44, which if approved by voters in November will restrict spending at nonprofit community health clinics (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits), as political leverage against the industry. Regan then offered to call off the measure if CPCA agreed to support the union’s efforts to unionize 25,000 industry workers, the lawsuit states.
Advertisement
In the complaint, CPCA estimates that 25,000 new union members would generate $2.37 million in monthly revenue from dues paid to UHW.
“This is about Dave Regan and UHW in particular adopting a strategy to create harmful legislation and harmful ballot initiatives to force people to the table to negotiate favorable agreements that will benefit them financially and then when those agreements don’t go through, they allow these initiatives to go through to create punishment for the organizations that can’t come to terms, and then they keep coming back, over and over and over again,” said Brandon Thornock, chief executive of plaintiff Shasta Community Health, echoing claims in the lawsuit.
“It’s a complete waste of resources and it’s amoral.”
A spokesperson for UHW did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. In an interview in July (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip), Regan denied asking the clinics to support his unionization efforts in exchange for dropping Proposition 44.
Advertisement
“We wanted to construct a relationship with the clinic association that prioritized appropriate funding of the community clinics in California, including restoring the healthcare cuts that were introduced by the ‘One Big [Beautiful] Bill,’” Regan said previously. “It was a strategic relationship where we’re working in a mutually cooperative way to properly fund the healthcare system to respect workers, and they were not interested in that.”

SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West President Dave Regan denied the allegations. He said he did not attempt to extort from union officials, or assault or threaten female labor leaders.
Sept. 11, 2026
Regan is a powerful figure in California politics who has a history of using the ballot box (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) to try to force the healthcare industry to unionize. The union leader has come under scrutiny this year (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find)over claims about his extreme political tactics, intimidating behavior toward and threats against women, and an allegation of assault more than 15 years ago, all of which he denies.
Regan is also the architect of California’s billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), a proposal on the November ballot to apply a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires that has splintered labor and divided Democrats. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-30/labor-organizers-spearheading-california-billionaire-tax-rebuffed-by-parent-union)
The CPCA lawsuit, in the federal court in the Eastern District of California, alleges that Regan’s political tactics are not designed to win initiatives, “but to subjugate and terrify.”
The union, the lawsuit states, has filed dozens of punitive ballot measures in California “targeting hospitals and dialysis providers with the implied threat or directly stated purpose of coercing health care providers into acquiescing to their union organizing or bargaining demands.” UHW has spent over $216 million, the suit says, on measures to “harm patients, destroy services, and drive providers out of business.” The vast majority of the UHW-backed measures have been withdrawn, usually after the industry agrees to concessions, the suit states.
“No other singular entity or individual has engaged in such widespread corruption of California’s initiative process,” the suit states.

### No on Proposition 44
The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
#### What is it?
Prop 44 penalizes certain nonprofit health clinics that spend less than 90% of their revenue on their mission.
The penalty equals the shortfall.
It covers nonprofit clinics that are federally qualified health centers, or FQHCs, plus "FQHC Look-Alikes" that meet the federal rules without getting an FQHC award.
Tribal and urban Indian organizations are excluded, and so are hospitals and private practices.
...
##### The 90% penalty
If a clinic's ratio comes in below 90%, the Department of Public Health charges a penalty equal to the whole gap: 90% of the clinic's total revenue, minus what it actually spent on its mission.
The measure never states the 90% figure as a spending mandate.
It enforces it through this penalty.
Penalty money goes into a state escrow account, and a clinic can ask the Department of Public Health for a waiver of the 90% requirement.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-dateline data-subscriber-content> SACRAMENTO — The California Primary Care Assn. and five clinics filed a civil lawsuit in federal court Friday accusing SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West and its president, Dave Regan, of racketeering and using ballot initiatives to “shake down” community health centers.
The association alleges that Regan and his union orchestrated a “multi-year campaign of coercion, threats, and economic pressure” to “extort” what the lawsuit describes as “valuable property rights” and “labor-organizing terms” from CPCA and the health centers the association represents in California, according to a copy of the complaint obtained by The Times.
The suit says Regan pushed Proposition 44, which if approved by voters in November will restrict spending at nonprofit community health clinics (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits), as political leverage against the industry. Regan then offered to call off the measure if CPCA agreed to support the union’s efforts to unionize 25,000 industry workers, the lawsuit states.
Advertisement
In the complaint, CPCA estimates that 25,000 new union members would generate $2.37 million in monthly revenue from dues paid to UHW.
“This is about Dave Regan and UHW in particular adopting a strategy to create harmful legislation and harmful ballot initiatives to force people to the table to negotiate favorable agreements that will benefit them financially and then when those agreements don’t go through, they allow these initiatives to go through to create punishment for the organizations that can’t come to terms, and then they keep coming back, over and over and over again,” said Brandon Thornock, chief executive of plaintiff Shasta Community Health, echoing claims in the lawsuit.
“It’s a complete waste of resources and it’s amoral.”
A spokesperson for UHW did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. In an interview in July (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip), Regan denied asking the clinics to support his unionization efforts in exchange for dropping Proposition 44.

“We wanted to construct a relationship with the clinic association that prioritized appropriate funding of the community clinics in California, including restoring the healthcare cuts that were introduced by the ‘One Big [Beautiful] Bill,’” Regan said previously. “It was a strategic relationship where we’re working in a mutually cooperative way to properly fund the healthcare system to respect workers, and they were not interested in that.”

“No other singular entity or individual has engaged in such widespread corruption of California’s initiative process,” the suit states.

### No on Proposition 44
The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
#### What is it?
Prop 44 penalizes certain nonprofit health clinics that spend less than 90% of their revenue on their mission.
The penalty equals the shortfall.
It covers nonprofit clinics that are federally qualified health centers, or FQHCs, plus "FQHC Look-Alikes" that meet the federal rules without getting an FQHC award.
Tribal and urban Indian organizations are excluded, and so are hospitals and private practices.
...
##### The 90% penalty
If a clinic's ratio comes in below 90%, the Department of Public Health charges a penalty equal to the whole gap: 90% of the clinic's total revenue, minus what it actually spent on its mission.
The measure never states the 90% figure as a spending mandate.
It enforces it through this penalty.
Penalty money goes into a state escrow account, and a clinic can ask the Department of Public Health for a waiver of the 90% requirement.

What is it?
Prop 44 penalizes certain nonprofit health clinics that spend less than 90% of their revenue on their mission. The penalty equals the shortfall.
It covers nonprofit clinics that are federally qualified health centers (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-clinic-definition), or FQHCs, plus "FQHC Look-Alikes" that meet the federal rules without getting an FQHC award. Tribal and urban Indian organizations are excluded, and so are hospitals and private practices.
Each covered clinic would send the Attorney General two numbers every year: what it spent on its mission, and its total revenue, both starting from figures the clinic already reports to the IRS. The Attorney General divides one by the other (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-mission-spend-ratio) to get a "Mission Spend Ratio," then publishes it.
The 90% penalty
If a clinic's ratio comes in below 90% (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-90-percent-penalty), the Department of Public Health charges a penalty equal to the whole gap: 90% of the clinic's total revenue, minus what it actually spent on its mission. The measure never states the 90% figure as a spending mandate. It enforces it through this penalty.
Penalty money goes into a state escrow account (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-penalty-account), and a clinic can ask the Department of Public Health for a waiver (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-economic-waiver) of the 90% requirement.
The measure's findings talk about clinic executive pay, but the operative sections do not cap or regulate pay. Executive pay counts against the ratio the same way any other non-program expense does.

Fiscal impacts
In its final analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf) for the state voter guide, the Legislative Analyst's Office estimates increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year to enforce the requirement, covered by fees charged to the affected clinics. The LAO notes clinics currently report spending an average of about 80% of revenue on providing health care services, below the measure's 90% line, so the penalty would apply widely. Other effects are uncertain and depend on how the Attorney General defines health care expenses and how clinics respond: some might spend more on patient services, raising state Medi-Cal costs, while others might close, shifting patients to publicly operated providers.
Why is this on the ballot?
Prop 44 is a signature-gathered statewide initiative, filed with the Attorney General's office as Initiative 25-0008. It originated with SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which says it targets clinics that divert revenue away from patient care toward executive pay and overhead.
According to Article II, Section 8 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%208.&article=II) of the California Constitution, citizens may introduce statutes (laws) by collecting signatures (5% of the votes cast in the most recent Governor's race). The statute must then be approved by voters with a simple majority of 50% + 1.

Official ballot title : "Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute." Fiscal impact label: "Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees."
Why vote No?
Prop 44 is SEIU-UHW's fourth try at regulating a healthcare industry by ballot measure, after voters rejected all three of its dialysis initiatives (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_23,_Dialysis_Clinic_Requirements_Initiative_%282020%29). The target this time is nonprofit community clinics, where operators say the union is organizing (https://fresnoland.org/2025/08/13/healthcare-initiative/), and the tool is a rule that every clinic spend at least 90% of its revenue on "mission-related expenses."
A 90% floor sounds reasonable. But everything else a clinic pays for has to fit into the other 10%, and the Legislative Analyst's Office found that clinics today average about 80% (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf), so most community clinics in the state would owe a penalty. That penalty is the entire shortfall (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-90-percent-penalty). The measure also never defines its central term: the Attorney General writes the definition after the election (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-ag-guidance), so a clinic that pays for patient vans or community outreach could be penalized like a profiteer. A labor dispute belongs at the bargaining table. Don't let it be settled by fining the clinics your neighbors depend on. Vote no.

Proposition 44 — The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Last Updated: September 8, 2026
No on Proposition 44
The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Read the Full Voter Guide (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/) Share
What is it?
Prop 44 penalizes certain nonprofit health clinics that spend less than 90% of their revenue on their mission. The penalty equals the shortfall.
It covers nonprofit clinics that are federally qualified health centers (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-clinic-definition), or FQHCs, plus "FQHC Look-Alikes" that meet the federal rules without getting an FQHC award. Tribal and urban Indian organizations are excluded, and so are hospitals and private practices.
Each covered clinic would send the Attorney General two numbers every year: what it spent on its mission, and its total revenue, both starting from figures the clinic already reports to the IRS. The Attorney General divides one by the other (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-mission-spend-ratio) to get a "Mission Spend Ratio," then publishes it.
The 90% penalty
If a clinic's ratio comes in below 90% (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-90-percent-penalty), the Department of Public Health charges a penalty equal to the whole gap: 90% of the clinic's total revenue, minus what it actually spent on its mission. The measure never states the 90% figure as a spending mandate. It enforces it through this penalty.
Penalty money goes into a state escrow account (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-penalty-account), and a clinic can ask the Department of Public Health for a waiver (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-economic-waiver) of the 90% requirement.
The measure's findings talk about clinic executive pay, but the operative sections do not cap or regulate pay. Executive pay counts against the ratio the same way any other non-program expense does.
Read the full annotated legal text → (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/)
Click to show fiscal impacts and more details Collapse details
Full legal text (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
Attorney General initiative page (25-0008) (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives)
Fiscal impacts
In its final analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf) for the state voter guide, the Legislative Analyst's Office estimates increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year to enforce the requirement, covered by fees charged to the affected clinics. The LAO notes clinics currently report spending an average of about 80% of revenue on providing health care services, below the measure's 90% line, so the penalty would apply widely. Other effects are uncertain and depend on how the Attorney General defines health care expenses and how clinics respond: some might spend more on patient services, raising state Medi-Cal costs, while others might close, shifting patients to publicly operated providers.
Why is this on the ballot?
Prop 44 is a signature-gathered statewide initiative, filed with the Attorney General's office as Initiative 25-0008. It originated with SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which says it targets clinics that divert revenue away from patient care toward executive pay and overhead.
According to Article II, Section 8 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%208.&article=II) of the California Constitution, citizens may introduce statutes (laws) by collecting signatures (5% of the votes cast in the most recent Governor's race). The statute must then be approved by voters with a simple majority of 50% + 1.
Placed on ballot by : Signature-gathered initiative petition; qualified in May 2026.
Official proponents : Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming, per Ballotpedia (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_44,_Spending_Requirements_for_Federally_Qualified_Health_Centers_Initiative_(2026)).
Sponsor and funder : SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_44,_Spending_Requirements_for_Federally_Qualified_Health_Centers_Initiative_(2026)) (SEIU-UHW West), through its committee Californians for Responsible Healthcare.
Official ballot title : "Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute." Fiscal impact label: "Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees."
Why vote No?
Prop 44 is SEIU-UHW's fourth try at regulating a healthcare industry by ballot measure, after voters rejected all three of its dialysis initiatives (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_23,_Dialysis_Clinic_Requirements_Initiative_%282020%29). The target this time is nonprofit community clinics, where operators say the union is organizing (https://fresnoland.org/2025/08/13/healthcare-initiative/), and the tool is a rule that every clinic spend at least 90% of its revenue on "mission-related expenses."
A 90% floor sounds reasonable. But everything else a clinic pays for has to fit into the other 10%, and the Legislative Analyst's Office found that clinics today average about 80% (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf), so most community clinics in the state would owe a penalty. That penalty is the entire shortfall (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-90-percent-penalty). The measure also never defines its central term: the Attorney General writes the definition after the election (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-ag-guidance), so a clinic that pays for patient vans or community outreach could be penalized like a profiteer. An analysis commissioned by the clinics (https://protectpatientsca.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) puts first-year penalties at $1.7B, and the clinics are suing in federal court (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/04/healthcare-workers-clinics-ballot-measure/) to stop it.
The people who actually run the safety net, the California Primary Care Association, the California Medical Association, and Planned Parenthood (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/), all oppose it, at a moment when federal Medicaid cuts are already squeezing clinics that serve 4.2 million Medi-Cal patients (https://kffhealthnews.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2026/05/Community-Clinic-complaint-vs.-SEIU-UHW-initiative.pdf). A labor dispute belongs at the bargaining table. Don't let it be settled by fining the clinics your neighbors depend on. Vote no.

> Proposition 44 — The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Proposition 44 — The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Last Updated: September 8, 2026
No on Proposition 44
The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Read the Full Voter Guide (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/) Share
What is it?
Prop 44 penalizes certain nonprofit health clinics that spend less than 90% of their revenue on their mission. The penalty equals the shortfall.
It covers nonprofit clinics that are federally qualified health centers (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-clinic-definition), or FQHCs, plus "FQHC Look-Alikes" that meet the federal rules without getting an FQHC award. Tribal and urban Indian organizations are excluded, and so are hospitals and private practices.
Each covered clinic would send the Attorney General two numbers every year: what it spent on its mission, and its total revenue, both starting from figures the clinic already reports to the IRS. The Attorney General divides one by the other (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-mission-spend-ratio) to get a "Mission Spend Ratio," then publishes it.
The 90% penalty
If a clinic's ratio comes in below 90% (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-90-percent-penalty), the Department of Public Health charges a penalty equal to the whole gap: 90% of the clinic's total revenue, minus what it actually spent on its mission. The measure never states the 90% figure as a spending mandate. It enforces it through this penalty.
Penalty money goes into a state escrow account (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-penalty-account), and a clinic can ask the Department of Public Health for a waiver (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-economic-waiver) of the 90% requirement.
The measure's findings talk about clinic executive pay, but the operative sections do not cap or regulate pay. Executive pay counts against the ratio the same way any other non-program expense does.
Read the full annotated legal text → (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/)
Click to show fiscal impacts and more details Collapse details
Full legal text (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
Attorney General initiative page (25-0008) (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives)
Fiscal impacts
In its final analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf) for the state voter guide, the Legislative Analyst's Office estimates increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year to enforce the requirement, covered by fees charged to the affected clinics. The LAO notes clinics currently report spending an average of about 80% of revenue on providing health care services, below the measure's 90% line, so the penalty would apply widely. Other effects are uncertain and depend on how the Attorney General defines health care expenses and how clinics respond: some might spend more on patient services, raising state Medi-Cal costs, while others might close, shifting patients to publicly operated providers.
Why is this on the ballot?
Prop 44 is a signature-gathered statewide initiative, filed with the Attorney General's office as Initiative 25-0008. It originated with SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which says it targets clinics that divert revenue away from patient care toward executive pay and overhead.
According to Article II, Section 8 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%208.&article=II) of the California Constitution, citizens may introduce statutes (laws) by collecting signatures (5% of the votes cast in the most recent Governor's race). The statute must then be approved by voters with a simple majority of 50% + 1.
Placed on ballot by : Signature-gathered initiative petition; qualified in May 2026.
Official proponents : Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming, per Ballotpedia (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_44,_Spending_Requirements_for_Federally_Qualified_Health_Centers_Initiative_(2026)).
Sponsor and funder : SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_44,_Spending_Requirements_for_Federally_Qualified_Health_Centers_Initiative_(2026)) (SEIU-UHW West), through its committee Californians for Responsible Healthcare.
Official ballot title : "Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute." Fiscal impact label: "Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees."
Why vote No?
Prop 44 is SEIU-UHW's fourth try at regulating a healthcare industry by ballot measure, after voters rejected all three of its dialysis initiatives (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_23,_Dialysis_Clinic_Requirements_Initiative_%282020%29). The target this time is nonprofit community clinics, where operators say the union is organizing (https://fresnoland.org/2025/08/13/healthcare-initiative/), and the tool is a rule that every clinic spend at least 90% of its revenue on "mission-related expenses."
A 90% floor sounds reasonable. But everything else a clinic pays for has to fit into the other 10%, and the Legislative Analyst's Office found that clinics today average about 80% (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf), so most community clinics in the state would owe a penalty. That penalty is the entire shortfall (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-90-percent-penalty). The measure also never defines its central term: the Attorney General writes the definition after the election (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-44/legal-text/#prop-44-ag-guidance), so a clinic that pays for patient vans or community outreach could be penalized like a profiteer. An analysis commissioned by the clinics (https://protectpatientsca.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) puts first-year penalties at $1.7B, and the clinics are suing in federal court (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/04/healthcare-workers-clinics-ballot-measure/) to stop it.
The people who actually run the safety net, the California Primary Care Association, the California Medical Association, and Planned Parenthood (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/), all oppose it, at a moment when federal Medicaid cuts are already squeezing clinics that serve 4.2 million Medi-Cal patients (https://kffhealthnews.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2026/05/Community-Clinic-complaint-vs.-SEIU-UHW-initiative.pdf). A labor dispute belongs at the bargaining table. Don't let it be settled by fining the clinics your neighbors depend on. Vote no.
Read the full voter guide (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/)

Proposition 44 pits California clinics against union known for ballot battles
By Ben Paviour
September 17, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The healthcare union behind a proposed California billionaire tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317240033.html) has a second, less-talked-about ballot measure with a different target: health clinics.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West’s Proposition 44 would require nonprofit, federally funded clinics that care for underserved populations to spend 90% of their revenues on services that advance their mission. If they don’t comply, they would face fines that would be returned to them if they hit the 90% spending target within five years.
The union argues that clinics are investing their revenue poorly, wasting it on everything from art to executive compensation of up to $1.9 million a year.
But its more numerous critics argue the measure represents an existential crisis for the clinics it purports to save. They say Prop. 44 is the latest in a series of ballot battles waged by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan that’s really aimed at creating leverage over employers in labor negotiations.
The backdrop for the fight is H.R. 1, the mixture of tax cuts and a Medicaid overhaul signed by President Donald Trump last year. That bill is expected to cause 2 million Californians to lose health insurance (https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/over-two-million-more-californians-projected-to-lack-health-insurance-by-2030/) by 2030, according to the UC Berkeley Labor Center.
SEIU-UHW argues that Prop. 44 will strengthen clinics by making them more accountable, while its critics say it will weaken them at a time of acute need.
While SEIU-UHW insists it will put resources behind the measure, the union hasn’t invested any major funds in Prop. 44 since May, instead funneling its dollars to support the billionaire tax. Opponents of the measure, meanwhile, had $32 million in cash on hand as of the end of June and have continued to raise money since then.
The proposition is one of the least popular of the 14 statewide measures on this year’s ballot, according to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317256476.html). Just 34% of the 1,745 California adults surveyed said they backed it.
Registered nurses Hope Wallen and John Bergmann rally against the cuts to Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, outside Rep. Kevin Kiley’s district office in Rocklin on Tuesday, July 1, 2025. The cuts are part of legislation in Congress known as President Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, which had passed the Senate earlier in the day and must now return to the House. HECTOR AMEZCUA hamezcua@sacbee.com
What clinics pass the Prop. 44 benchmark?
At its heart, Prop. 44 centers on tax returns that every nonprofit files with the federal government.
Clinics and other nonprofits are required to report how much revenue they make and how much they spend on program services. Prop. 44 uses that number as the baseline for its calculation of “mission spend ratio.” The California attorney general could modify what is or isn’t included on that list that would count toward the 90% spending on program services.
Brad Fulton, head of Indiana University’s Philanthropy Research Hub who is not involved in the fight, assessed the potential impact of Prop. 44 at the request of The Sacramento Bee using their tax returns.
Fulton found that 89% of the 147 California clinic organizations (many of which operate multiple clinics) would fail to meet Prop. 44’s spending threshold and face $1.6 billion in first year fines. Of the 16 organizations that did meet it, all but two had finances in the red, suggesting they are financially distressed. Fulton argued the proposition effectively would limit clinics from accumulating surpluses and reserves.
“Almost no health center in the U.S. meets Prop. 44’s standard,” Fulton wrote.
California Primary Care Association President Francisco Silva said clinics anticipated the growing need for their services, pointing to the effects of HR 1.
“This is the time to actually grow health centers so we can serve that patient base, not to cut them back,” Silva said in an interview.
Both the Democratic and Republican state parties formally adopted a “no” stance on Prop. 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html). Other organizations opposed to the measure include Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the California Teachers Association and the California Chamber of Commerce.
The only group to endorse Prop. 44 beyond its sponsor is the California Federation of Labor.
Spokesperson Renée Saldaña said she expected more organizations to join the coalition. She said the measure is designed to hold taxpayer-funded clinics to a higher standard.
“We want to cut what we see as wasteful spending and redirect that money so that patients can access this care when they need it,” Saldaña said in an interview.
The fight behind the fight
Prop. 44 wound up on the ballot after a breakdown in negotiations between Regan, the SEIU-UHW president, and Silva’s California Primary Care Association.
Silva said those negotiations centered on unionization efforts at clinics rather than the clinic spending at the center of Prop. 44 — proof, he contends, of Regan’s true intentions with the measure.
SEIU-UHW has often filed ballot measures for organizations that have resisted its unionization efforts, including a series of recent measures that would have placed new regulations on dialysis clinics.
SEIU-UHW healthcare workers protest layoffs, relocations and wage proposals outside Kaiser Permanente on Wednesday May 2, 2018 in Sacramento. Paul Kitagaki Jr. pkitagaki@sacbee.com
The union has increasingly turned its attention to clinics, some of which are already unionized.
It initially sought to pass a version of Prop. 44 through the Legislature. Its 2025 bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1113), which failed to pass, would have exempted clinics that set up “labor-management cooperation committees” from the 90% threshold.
“The emergency is here now,” Saldaña said. “Clinics are already closing and so we took it directly to the voters.”
Some clinics that would be affected by Prop. 44 have fought unionization efforts. For example, Innercare, which operates more than a dozen health and dental clinics across the state, spent more than $577,000 on a consulting firm that aimed to discourage workers from joining the union in 2024, according to federal filings.
The National Labor Relations Board is currently considering allegations that Innercare illegally harassed and terminated employees during the 2024 unionization drive. SEIU-UHW alleges that Innercare retaliated against pro-union workers, offered perks to anti-union workers and engaged in unlawful surveillance.
Innercare Executive Vice President Young Kwon said in a statement that more than 60% of the workers voted against joining the union and that the company is “committed to fostering a respectful, lawful and supportive workplace.”
“Innercare denies that it engaged in unlawful conduct or violated employees’ rights under federal labor law in any way,” Kwon said.
Prop. 44 critics like Silva those fights shouldn’t be lumped together with the ballot measure, which wouldn’t change anything about clinic unionization.
“It’s an accusation to distract from what’s really in front of the voters,” he said.

- SEIU-UHW calls the measure legally sound

Capitol Alert (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/)
Proposition 44 pits California clinics against union known for ballot battles
By Ben Paviour
September 17, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The healthcare union behind a proposed California billionaire tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317240033.html) has a second, less-talked-about ballot measure with a different target: health clinics.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West’s Proposition 44 would require nonprofit, federally funded clinics that care for underserved populations to spend 90% of their revenues on services that advance their mission. If they don’t comply, they would face fines that would be returned to them if they hit the 90% spending target within five years.
The union argues that clinics are investing their revenue poorly, wasting it on everything from art to executive compensation of up to $1.9 million a year.
But its more numerous critics argue the measure represents an existential crisis for the clinics it purports to save. They say Prop. 44 is the latest in a series of ballot battles waged by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan that’s really aimed at creating leverage over employers in labor negotiations.
The backdrop for the fight is H.R. 1, the mixture of tax cuts and a Medicaid overhaul signed by President Donald Trump last year. That bill is expected to cause 2 million Californians to lose health insurance (https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/over-two-million-more-californians-projected-to-lack-health-insurance-by-2030/) by 2030, according to the UC Berkeley Labor Center.
SEIU-UHW argues that Prop. 44 will strengthen clinics by making them more accountable, while its critics say it will weaken them at a time of acute need.
While SEIU-UHW insists it will put resources behind the measure, the union hasn’t invested any major funds in Prop. 44 since May, instead funneling its dollars to support the billionaire tax. Opponents of the measure, meanwhile, had $32 million in cash on hand as of the end of June and have continued to raise money since then.
The proposition is one of the least popular of the 14 statewide measures on this year’s ballot, according to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317256476.html). Just 34% of the 1,745 California adults surveyed said they backed it.
Registered nurses Hope Wallen and John Bergmann rally against the cuts to Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, outside Rep. Kevin Kiley’s district office in Rocklin on Tuesday, July 1, 2025. The cuts are part of legislation in Congress known as President Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, which had passed the Senate earlier in the day and must now return to the House. HECTOR AMEZCUA hamezcua@sacbee.com
What clinics pass the Prop. 44 benchmark?
At its heart, Prop. 44 centers on tax returns that every nonprofit files with the federal government.
Clinics and other nonprofits are required to report how much revenue they make and how much they spend on program services. Prop. 44 uses that number as the baseline for its calculation of “mission spend ratio.” The California attorney general could modify what is or isn’t included on that list that would count toward the 90% spending on program services.
Brad Fulton, head of Indiana University’s Philanthropy Research Hub who is not involved in the fight, assessed the potential impact of Prop. 44 at the request of The Sacramento Bee using their tax returns.
Fulton found that 89% of the 147 California clinic organizations (many of which operate multiple clinics) would fail to meet Prop. 44’s spending threshold and face $1.6 billion in first year fines. Of the 16 organizations that did meet it, all but two had finances in the red, suggesting they are financially distressed. Fulton argued the proposition effectively would limit clinics from accumulating surpluses and reserves.
“Almost no health center in the U.S. meets Prop. 44’s standard,” Fulton wrote.
California Primary Care Association President Francisco Silva said clinics anticipated the growing need for their services, pointing to the effects of HR 1.
“This is the time to actually grow health centers so we can serve that patient base, not to cut them back,” Silva said in an interview.
Both the Democratic and Republican state parties formally adopted a “no” stance on Prop. 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html). Other organizations opposed to the measure include Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the California Teachers Association and the California Chamber of Commerce.
The only group to endorse Prop. 44 beyond its sponsor is the California Federation of Labor.
Spokesperson Renée Saldaña said she expected more organizations to join the coalition. She said the measure is designed to hold taxpayer-funded clinics to a higher standard.
“We want to cut what we see as wasteful spending and redirect that money so that patients can access this care when they need it,” Saldaña said in an interview.
The fight behind the fight
Prop. 44 wound up on the ballot after a breakdown in negotiations between Regan, the SEIU-UHW president, and Silva’s California Primary Care Association.
Silva said those negotiations centered on unionization efforts at clinics rather than the clinic spending at the center of Prop. 44 — proof, he contends, of Regan’s true intentions with the measure.
SEIU-UHW has often filed ballot measures for organizations that have resisted its unionization efforts, including a series of recent measures that would have placed new regulations on dialysis clinics.
SEIU-UHW healthcare workers protest layoffs, relocations and wage proposals outside Kaiser Permanente on Wednesday May 2, 2018 in Sacramento. Paul Kitagaki Jr. pkitagaki@sacbee.com
The union has increasingly turned its attention to clinics, some of which are already unionized.
It initially sought to pass a version of Prop. 44 through the Legislature. Its 2025 bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1113), which failed to pass, would have exempted clinics that set up “labor-management cooperation committees” from the 90% threshold.
“The emergency is here now,” Saldaña said. “Clinics are already closing and so we took it directly to the voters.”
Some clinics that would be affected by Prop. 44 have fought unionization efforts. For example, Innercare, which operates more than a dozen health and dental clinics across the state, spent more than $577,000 on a consulting firm that aimed to discourage workers from joining the union in 2024, according to federal filings.
The National Labor Relations Board is currently considering allegations that Innercare illegally harassed and terminated employees during the 2024 unionization drive. SEIU-UHW alleges that Innercare retaliated against pro-union workers, offered perks to anti-union workers and engaged in unlawful surveillance.
Innercare Executive Vice President Young Kwon said in a statement that more than 60% of the workers voted against joining the union and that the company is “committed to fostering a respectful, lawful and supportive workplace.”
“Innercare denies that it engaged in unlawful conduct or violated employees’ rights under federal labor law in any way,” Kwon said.
Prop. 44 critics like Silva those fights shouldn’t be lumped together with the ballot measure, which wouldn’t change anything about clinic unionization.
“It’s an accusation to distract from what’s really in front of the voters,” he said.
