If they don’t comply, they would face fines that would be returned to them if they hit the 90% spending target within five years.
The union argues that clinics are investing their revenue poorly, wasting it on everything from art to executive compensation of up to $1.9 million a year.
But its more numerous critics argue the measure represents an existential crisis for the clinics it purports to save. They say Prop. 44 is the latest in a series of ballot battles waged by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan that’s really aimed at creating leverage over employers in labor negotiations.
The backdrop for the fight is H.R. 1, the mixture of tax cuts and a Medicaid overhaul signed by President Donald Trump last year. That bill is expected to cause 2 million Californians to lose health insurance (https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/over-two-million-more-californians-projected-to-lack-health-insurance-by-2030/) by 2030, according to the UC Berkeley Labor Center.
SEIU-UHW argues that Prop. 44 will strengthen clinics by making them more accountable, while its critics say it will weaken them at a time of acute need.
While SEIU-UHW insists it will put resources behind the measure, the union hasn’t invested any major funds in Prop. 44 since May, instead funneling its dollars to support the billionaire tax. Opponents of the measure, meanwhile, had $32 million in cash on hand as of the end of June and have continued to raise money since then.
The proposition is one of the least popular of the 14 statewide measures on this year’s ballot, according to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317256476.html). Just 34% of the 1,745 California adults surveyed said they backed it.
Registered nurses Hope Wallen and John Bergmann rally against the cuts to Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, outside Rep. Kevin Kiley’s district office in Rocklin on Tuesday, July 1, 2025. The cuts are part of legislation in Congress known as President Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, which had passed the Senate earlier in the day and must now return to the House. HECTOR AMEZCUA hamezcua@sacbee.com
What clinics pass the Prop. 44 benchmark?
At its heart, Prop. 44 centers on tax returns that every nonprofit files with the federal government.
Clinics and other nonprofits are required to report how much revenue they make and how much they spend on program services. Prop. 44 uses that number as the baseline for its calculation of “mission spend ratio.” The California attorney general could modify what is or isn’t included on that list that would count toward the 90% spending on program services.
Brad Fulton, head of Indiana University’s Philanthropy Research Hub who is not involved in the fight, assessed the potential impact of Prop. 44 at the request of The Sacramento Bee using their tax returns.
Fulton found that 89% of the 147 California clinic organizations (many of which operate multiple clinics) would fail to meet Prop. 44’s spending threshold and face $1.6 billion in first year fines. Of the 16 organizations that did meet it, all but two had finances in the red, suggesting they are financially distressed. Fulton argued the proposition effectively would limit clinics from accumulating surpluses and reserves.
“Almost no health center in the U.S. meets Prop. 44’s standard,” Fulton wrote.
California Primary Care Association President Francisco Silva said clinics anticipated the growing need for their services, pointing to the effects of HR 1.
“This is the time to actually grow health centers so we can serve that patient base, not to cut them back,” Silva said in an interview.
Both the Democratic and Republican state parties formally adopted a “no” stance on Prop. 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html). Other organizations opposed to the measure include Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the California Teachers Association and the California Chamber of Commerce.
The only group to endorse Prop. 44 beyond its sponsor is the California Federation of Labor.
Spokesperson Renée Saldaña said she expected more organizations to join the coalition. She said the measure is designed to hold taxpayer-funded clinics to a higher standard.
“We want to cut what we see as wasteful spending and redirect that money so that patients can access this care when they need it,” Saldaña said in an interview.
The fight behind the fight
Prop. 44 wound up on the ballot after a breakdown in negotiations between Regan, the SEIU-UHW president, and Silva’s California Primary Care Association.
Silva said those negotiations centered on unionization efforts at clinics rather than the clinic spending at the center of Prop. 44 — proof, he contends, of Regan’s true intentions with the measure.
SEIU-UHW has often filed ballot measures for organizations that have resisted its unionization efforts, including a series of recent measures that would have placed new regulations on dialysis clinics.
SEIU-UHW healthcare workers protest layoffs, relocations and wage proposals outside Kaiser Permanente on Wednesday May 2, 2018 in Sacramento. Paul Kitagaki Jr. pkitagaki@sacbee.com
The union has increasingly turned its attention to clinics, some of which are already unionized.
It initially sought to pass a version of Prop. 44 through the Legislature. Its 2025 bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1113), which failed to pass, would have exempted clinics that set up “labor-management cooperation committees” from the 90% threshold.
“The emergency is here now,” Saldaña said. “Clinics are already closing and so we took it directly to the voters.”
Some clinics that would be affected by Prop. 44 have fought unionization efforts. For example, Innercare, which operates more than a dozen health and dental clinics across the state, spent more than $577,000 on a consulting firm that aimed to discourage workers from joining the union in 2024, according to federal filings.
The National Labor Relations Board is currently considering allegations that Innercare illegally harassed and terminated employees during the 2024 unionization drive. SEIU-UHW alleges that Innercare retaliated against pro-union workers, offered perks to anti-union workers and engaged in unlawful surveillance.
Innercare Executive Vice President Young Kwon said in a statement that more than 60% of the workers voted against joining the union and that the company is “committed to fostering a respectful, lawful and supportive workplace.”
“Innercare denies that it engaged in unlawful conduct or violated employees’ rights under federal labor law in any way,” Kwon said.
Prop. 44 critics like Silva those fights shouldn’t be lumped together with the ballot measure, which wouldn’t change anything about clinic unionization.
“It’s an accusation to distract from what’s really in front of the voters,” he said.

Proposition 44 pits California clinics against union known for ballot battles
By Ben Paviour
September 17, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The healthcare union behind a proposed California billionaire tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317240033.html) has a second, less-talked-about ballot measure with a different target: health clinics.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West’s Proposition 44 would require nonprofit, federally funded clinics that care for underserved populations to spend 90% of their revenues on services that advance their mission. If they don’t comply, they would face fines that would be returned to them if they hit the 90% spending target within five years.
The union argues that clinics are investing their revenue poorly, wasting it on everything from art to executive compensation of up to $1.9 million a year.
But its more numerous critics argue the measure represents an existential crisis for the clinics it purports to save. They say Prop. 44 is the latest in a series of ballot battles waged by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan that’s really aimed at creating leverage over employers in labor negotiations.
The backdrop for the fight is H.R. 1, the mixture of tax cuts and a Medicaid overhaul signed by President Donald Trump last year. That bill is expected to cause 2 million Californians to lose health insurance (https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/over-two-million-more-californians-projected-to-lack-health-insurance-by-2030/) by 2030, according to the UC Berkeley Labor Center.
SEIU-UHW argues that Prop. 44 will strengthen clinics by making them more accountable, while its critics say it will weaken them at a time of acute need.
While SEIU-UHW insists it will put resources behind the measure, the union hasn’t invested any major funds in Prop. 44 since May, instead funneling its dollars to support the billionaire tax. Opponents of the measure, meanwhile, had $32 million in cash on hand as of the end of June and have continued to raise money since then.
The proposition is one of the least popular of the 14 statewide measures on this year’s ballot, according to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317256476.html). Just 34% of the 1,745 California adults surveyed said they backed it.
Registered nurses Hope Wallen and John Bergmann rally against the cuts to Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, outside Rep. Kevin Kiley’s district office in Rocklin on Tuesday, July 1, 2025. The cuts are part of legislation in Congress known as President Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, which had passed the Senate earlier in the day and must now return to the House. HECTOR AMEZCUA hamezcua@sacbee.com
What clinics pass the Prop. 44 benchmark?
At its heart, Prop. 44 centers on tax returns that every nonprofit files with the federal government.
Clinics and other nonprofits are required to report how much revenue they make and how much they spend on program services. Prop. 44 uses that number as the baseline for its calculation of “mission spend ratio.” The California attorney general could modify what is or isn’t included on that list that would count toward the 90% spending on program services.
Brad Fulton, head of Indiana University’s Philanthropy Research Hub who is not involved in the fight, assessed the potential impact of Prop. 44 at the request of The Sacramento Bee using their tax returns.
Fulton found that 89% of the 147 California clinic organizations (many of which operate multiple clinics) would fail to meet Prop. 44’s spending threshold and face $1.6 billion in first year fines. Of the 16 organizations that did meet it, all but two had finances in the red, suggesting they are financially distressed. Fulton argued the proposition effectively would limit clinics from accumulating surpluses and reserves.
“Almost no health center in the U.S. meets Prop. 44’s standard,” Fulton wrote.
California Primary Care Association President Francisco Silva said clinics anticipated the growing need for their services, pointing to the effects of HR 1.
“This is the time to actually grow health centers so we can serve that patient base, not to cut them back,” Silva said in an interview.
Both the Democratic and Republican state parties formally adopted a “no” stance on Prop. 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html). Other organizations opposed to the measure include Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the California Teachers Association and the California Chamber of Commerce.
The only group to endorse Prop. 44 beyond its sponsor is the California Federation of Labor.
Spokesperson Renée Saldaña said she expected more organizations to join the coalition. She said the measure is designed to hold taxpayer-funded clinics to a higher standard.
“We want to cut what we see as wasteful spending and redirect that money so that patients can access this care when they need it,” Saldaña said in an interview.
The fight behind the fight
Prop. 44 wound up on the ballot after a breakdown in negotiations between Regan, the SEIU-UHW president, and Silva’s California Primary Care Association.
Silva said those negotiations centered on unionization efforts at clinics rather than the clinic spending at the center of Prop. 44 — proof, he contends, of Regan’s true intentions with the measure.
SEIU-UHW has often filed ballot measures for organizations that have resisted its unionization efforts, including a series of recent measures that would have placed new regulations on dialysis clinics.
SEIU-UHW healthcare workers protest layoffs, relocations and wage proposals outside Kaiser Permanente on Wednesday May 2, 2018 in Sacramento. Paul Kitagaki Jr. pkitagaki@sacbee.com
The union has increasingly turned its attention to clinics, some of which are already unionized.
It initially sought to pass a version of Prop. 44 through the Legislature. Its 2025 bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1113), which failed to pass, would have exempted clinics that set up “labor-management cooperation committees” from the 90% threshold.
“The emergency is here now,” Saldaña said. “Clinics are already closing and so we took it directly to the voters.”
Some clinics that would be affected by Prop. 44 have fought unionization efforts. For example, Innercare, which operates more than a dozen health and dental clinics across the state, spent more than $577,000 on a consulting firm that aimed to discourage workers from joining the union in 2024, according to federal filings.
The National Labor Relations Board is currently considering allegations that Innercare illegally harassed and terminated employees during the 2024 unionization drive. SEIU-UHW alleges that Innercare retaliated against pro-union workers, offered perks to anti-union workers and engaged in unlawful surveillance.
Innercare Executive Vice President Young Kwon said in a statement that more than 60% of the workers voted against joining the union and that the company is “committed to fostering a respectful, lawful and supportive workplace.”
“Innercare denies that it engaged in unlawful conduct or violated employees’ rights under federal labor law in any way,” Kwon said.
Prop. 44 critics like Silva those fights shouldn’t be lumped together with the ballot measure, which wouldn’t change anything about clinic unionization.
“It’s an accusation to distract from what’s really in front of the voters,” he said.

Proposition 44 would lay greater restrictions on how California health centers use revenue, which some centers say is actually creating an unlawful state-operated auditing process.
SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — A magistrate judge found two California health center organizations can't sue to stop California Secretary of State Shirley Weber from placing an initiative on revenue use on November's ballot.
Magistrate Judge Alex Tse said the suit over Proposition 44 failed on standing rather than questions of constitutionality.
'Plaintiffs cite to no authority in support of their position,' Tse wrote in his 14-page ruling.
'Plaintiffs concede Weber has no duty (statutory or otherwise) to review ballot initiatives for their constitutionality.

California Prop 44 guide: A 90% spending rule for community health clinics, backed by a union and opposed by the clinics themselves
Proposition 44 would require California’s nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services or pay the shortfall as a penalty. Here is how the ratio works, what it shows for seven large clinics, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026
Link copied!

California's community health clinics are facing a 90% spending rule under Proposition 44, which would penalize nonprofit clinics that spend less on patient services.
Proposition 44 would require California's nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue each year on patient services and the work that supports them, or pay the difference to the state as a penalty. The clinics it covers are Federally Qualified Health Centers: the network of safety-net clinics that provide primary, dental and mental health care to low-income and uninsured patients, many of them on Medi-Cal. Prop 44 is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/) placed on the ballot by petition, and its sponsor and sole funder is SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, a health care workers union. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it trails by 27 points in the only poll that has tested it: 34% yes and 61% no in PPIC's September survey, with nearly identical margins among Democrats, Republicans and independents.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The fight is between a union and the clinics it would regulate. The Legislative Analyst's Office says California's safety-net clinics report spending "an average of about 80 percent" of revenue on health care services, so most would start below the line. Supporters say the rule moves money from executive pay and overhead to patients; opponents, led by the clinics' own trade association, say it would close clinics. This explainer covers what the text requires, how the 90% ratio is calculated, what it shows for seven of the clinics paying to defeat it, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.

California Prop 44 guide: A 90% spending rule for community health clinics, backed by a union and opposed by the clinics themselves
Proposition 44 would require California’s nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services or pay the shortfall as a penalty. Here is how the ratio works, what it shows for seven large clinics, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026
Link copied!

California's community health clinics are facing a 90% spending rule under Proposition 44, which would penalize nonprofit clinics that spend less on patient services.
Proposition 44 would require California's nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue each year on patient services and the work that supports them, or pay the difference to the state as a penalty. The clinics it covers are Federally Qualified Health Centers: the network of safety-net clinics that provide primary, dental and mental health care to low-income and uninsured patients, many of them on Medi-Cal. Prop 44 is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/) placed on the ballot by petition, and its sponsor and sole funder is SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, a health care workers union. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it trails by 27 points in the only poll that has tested it: 34% yes and 61% no in PPIC's September survey, with nearly identical margins among Democrats, Republicans and independents.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The fight is between a union and the clinics it would regulate. The Legislative Analyst's Office says California's safety-net clinics report spending "an average of about 80 percent" of revenue on health care services, so most would start below the line. Supporters say the rule moves money from executive pay and overhead to patients; opponents, led by the clinics' own trade association, say it would close clinics. This explainer covers what the text requires, how the 90% ratio is calculated, what it shows for seven of the clinics paying to defeat it, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.

California Prop 44 guide: A 90% spending rule for community health clinics, backed by a union and opposed by the clinics themselves
Proposition 44 would require California’s nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services or pay the shortfall as a penalty. Here is how the ratio works, what it shows for seven large clinics, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.
by

Updated

California's community health clinics are facing a 90% spending rule under Proposition 44, which would penalize nonprofit clinics that spend less on patient services.
Proposition 44 would require California's nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue each year on patient services and the work that supports them, or pay the difference to the state as a penalty. The clinics it covers are Federally Qualified Health Centers: the network of safety-net clinics that provide primary, dental and mental health care to low-income and uninsured patients, many of them on Medi-Cal. Prop 44 is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/) placed on the ballot by petition, and its sponsor and sole funder is SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, a health care workers union. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it trails by 27 points in the only poll that has tested it: 34% yes and 61% no in PPIC's September survey, with nearly identical margins among Democrats, Republicans and independents.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The fight is between a union and the clinics it would regulate. The Legislative Analyst's Office says California's safety-net clinics report spending "an average of about 80 percent" of revenue on health care services, so most would start below the line. Supporters say the rule moves money from executive pay and overhead to patients; opponents, led by the clinics' own trade association, say it would close clinics. This explainer covers what the text requires, how the 90% ratio is calculated, what it shows for seven of the clinics paying to defeat it, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.

California Prop 44 guide: A 90% spending rule for community health clinics, backed by a union and opposed by the clinics themselves
Proposition 44 would require California’s nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services or pay the shortfall as a penalty. Here is how the ratio works, what it shows for seven large clinics, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.
by

Updated

California's community health clinics are facing a 90% spending rule under Proposition 44, which would penalize nonprofit clinics that spend less on patient services.
Proposition 44 would require California's nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue each year on patient services and the work that supports them, or pay the difference to the state as a penalty. The clinics it covers are Federally Qualified Health Centers: the network of safety-net clinics that provide primary, dental and mental health care to low-income and uninsured patients, many of them on Medi-Cal. Prop 44 is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/) placed on the ballot by petition, and its sponsor and sole funder is SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, a health care workers union. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it trails by 27 points in the only poll that has tested it: 34% yes and 61% no in PPIC's September survey, with nearly identical margins among Democrats, Republicans and independents.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The fight is between a union and the clinics it would regulate. The Legislative Analyst's Office says California's safety-net clinics report spending "an average of about 80 percent" of revenue on health care services, so most would start below the line. Supporters say the rule moves money from executive pay and overhead to patients; opponents, led by the clinics' own trade association, say it would close clinics. This explainer covers what the text requires, how the 90% ratio is calculated, what it shows for seven of the clinics paying to defeat it, what the LAO says it costs, and who is funding each side.

Proposition 44 sets a 90% "Mission Spend Ratio" for nonprofit community health clinics
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop44-text-proposed-laws.pdf) introduces a single number, the "Mission Spend Ratio": the total a clinic spends on "activities that accomplish each clinic's exempt purpose" divided by its total revenue. A clinic below 90% owes a penalty.
The measure applies to private nonprofit clinic corporations that are Federally Qualified Health Centers under federal Medicaid law, including "FQHC look-alikes," clinics that meet the federal program's requirements without receiving its grant. It excludes clinics run by federally recognized tribes, tribal organizations and urban Indian organizations. Public clinics, such as those run by counties, are not covered; the LAO describes the rule as applying to "private nonprofit safety net clinics."
The starting figures come from each clinic's federal tax return. The text says spending on the clinic's purpose "will be based on" the "total program service expenses" on line 4e of Part III of IRS Form 990, and revenue on line 12 of Part I, both "as of calendar year 2024." From there the Attorney General may issue "binding guidance" that adjusts both numbers: counting some spending the 990 does not classify as program services, excluding some that it does, and tightening the reporting of payments to "related parties" such as management companies, landlords and affiliated foundations, so that money routed through them cannot inflate the ratio. The Attorney General must publish findings explaining that guidance and can issue it through bulletins rather than formal regulations.
Each clinic files the data with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers every year. Within 90 days the Attorney General calculates every clinic's ratio, sends it to the clinic and the California Department of Public Health, and posts it online. Clinics pay a new annual fee set to cover the cost of running the program.
The 10% left over must cover administration and any surplus
Because the ratio is measured against revenue rather than spending, the remaining 10% has to absorb two different things: everything the clinic spends outside program services, such as administration, finance, human resources and fundraising, and any money it takes in but does not spend that year. A clinic that runs a surplus to build reserves or save for a new building lowers its ratio by exactly that amount, even if its spending is all on patient care.
That design is deliberate. The measure's findings say some clinics report management and administrative expenses of "30 to 40 percent of total revenue" while others spend under 10%, and that "many clinics are highly profitable, sometimes reporting annual surpluses of as much as 20 percent of total revenue, rather than spending the funds in a manner consistent with their charitable mission." Its stated intent is "a reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed spending as a proportion of total revenue."
What counts as patient care is the contested part. The Yes campaign's rebuttal says qualifying spending "CAN INCLUDE" transportation, interpretation, care coordination, outreach, nurse managers, medical equipment and information technology. The No argument says the measure "restricts clinics from funding mammogram, X-ray and CT machines, information technology and expanding or upgrading clinics." The text settles neither claim; it leaves the line to the Attorney General's guidance. The LAO says the outcome of that guidance is one of two things its cost estimate depends on.
Rule Today Under Proposition 44
Spending floor No minimum share of revenue that must go to patient services At least 90% of total revenue on “program services” each fiscal year
What counts Clinics classify their own expenses on IRS Form 990 Form 990 program expenses divided by total revenue, adjusted by binding Attorney General guidance
Falling short No state penalty tied to a spending ratio Penalty equal to the gap to 90%, paid to the Department of Public Health
Getting money back Not applicable Refund if the clinic reaches 90% within five years and agrees on a spending plan; otherwise the money goes to clinic workforce programs
Public reporting Form 990 to the IRS and annual reports to the Attorney General’s Registry of Charities Plus Mission Spend Ratio data; the Attorney General posts each clinic’s ratio within 90 days
Relief Not applicable One-year waivers for unexpected circumstances or a threat to the clinic’s survival as a going concern
Enforcement Attorney General oversight of charities Any patient may sue for breach of charitable trust; fines of $5,000, then $10,000 a month, for late reports; jail for knowing misreporting
Who is covered Not applicable Private nonprofit FQHCs and FQHC look-alikes; tribal and urban Indian clinics excluded
Start date Not applicable Each clinic’s first full fiscal year beginning at least six months after passage
Seven clinics funding the No campaign: Mission Spend Ratios from 64.5% to 83.9%
To show what the ratio looks like in practice, we applied the measure's starting formula to the 2024 Form 990s of seven clinics on the No campaign's list of top contributors at the Fair Political Practices Commission. Together they reported $3.28 billion in revenue. On the measure's starting numbers, none reaches 90%: their combined ratio is 77.4%, and the gap to 90% totals $412.5 million.
AltaMed, the No campaign's largest donor and the largest of the seven at $1.72 billion in revenue, spent $1.44 billion on program services, a ratio of 83.9% and a gap of $105.2 million. Family Health Centers of San Diego has the lowest ratio, 64.5%, and the largest gap, $124.6 million. The others: WellSpace Health 77.9% ($20.7 million), TrueCare 73.8% ($21.2 million), North East Medical Services 73.5% ($63.5 million), Neighborhood Healthcare 72.0% ($48.7 million) and Innercare 64.7% ($28.6 million).
The reasons differ, which is why the revenue breakdown matters. Innercare's management and fundraising expenses equal 29.8% of its revenue, the highest of the seven. WellSpace Health spent 93.5% of its total expenses on program services but ran a surplus equal to 16.6% of revenue, so its ratio falls to 77.9%. Family Health Centers of San Diego (16.3%) and Neighborhood Healthcare (14.4%) also ran double-digit surpluses. AltaMed's surplus was 4.0% of revenue.
Proposition 44's Mission Spend Ratio is falling short of 90% at seven community health clinics funding the No campaign, on their 2024 tax returns before any Attorney General adjustments. These figures come with limits. They are the measure's starting point, before any guidance from the Attorney General, which could raise or lower every ratio. The seven are large clinics that chose to fund the opposition, not a sample of California's health centers. Three report on a July–June fiscal year, so their "2024" return covers July 2024 through June 2025. And a single year's revenue can include capital grants or investment gains that swell the surplus. The statewide reads come from the LAO: an average of about 80% on health care services, and "most FQHCs spend less than 90 percent," in the words of its September 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0008A1%29.pdf) to the Attorney General.
The same filings report executive pay, the Yes campaign's main target. AltaMed's president and chief executive, Castulo de la Rocha, received $1,949,272 in total compensation in 2024, according to the return's Schedule J. North East Medical Services reported $1,950,174 for its president and chief executive, Eddie Chan, $1,054,094 of it retirement and deferred compensation. The chief executives of TrueCare, Neighborhood Healthcare and Innercare reported $667,101 to $729,864.
Proposition 44's penalties: Refundable for five years, then spent on the clinic workforce

Proposition 44 sets a 90% "Mission Spend Ratio" for nonprofit community health clinics
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop44-text-proposed-laws.pdf) introduces a single number, the "Mission Spend Ratio": the total a clinic spends on "activities that accomplish each clinic's exempt purpose" divided by its total revenue. A clinic below 90% owes a penalty.
The measure applies to private nonprofit clinic corporations that are Federally Qualified Health Centers under federal Medicaid law, including "FQHC look-alikes," clinics that meet the federal program's requirements without receiving its grant. It excludes clinics run by federally recognized tribes, tribal organizations and urban Indian organizations. Public clinics, such as those run by counties, are not covered; the LAO describes the rule as applying to "private nonprofit safety net clinics."
The starting figures come from each clinic's federal tax return. The text says spending on the clinic's purpose "will be based on" the "total program service expenses" on line 4e of Part III of IRS Form 990, and revenue on line 12 of Part I, both "as of calendar year 2024." From there the Attorney General may issue "binding guidance" that adjusts both numbers: counting some spending the 990 does not classify as program services, excluding some that it does, and tightening the reporting of payments to "related parties" such as management companies, landlords and affiliated foundations, so that money routed through them cannot inflate the ratio. The Attorney General must publish findings explaining that guidance and can issue it through bulletins rather than formal regulations.
Each clinic files the data with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers every year. Within 90 days the Attorney General calculates every clinic's ratio, sends it to the clinic and the California Department of Public Health, and posts it online. Clinics pay a new annual fee set to cover the cost of running the program.

Because the ratio is measured against revenue rather than spending, the remaining 10% has to absorb two different things: everything the clinic spends outside program services, such as administration, finance, human resources and fundraising, and any money it takes in but does not spend that year. A clinic that runs a surplus to build reserves or save for a new building lowers its ratio by exactly that amount, even if its spending is all on patient care.
That design is deliberate. The measure's findings say some clinics report management and administrative expenses of "30 to 40 percent of total revenue" while others spend under 10%, and that "many clinics are highly profitable, sometimes reporting annual surpluses of as much as 20 percent of total revenue, rather than spending the funds in a manner consistent with their charitable mission." Its stated intent is "a reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed spending as a proportion of total revenue."
What counts as patient care is the contested part. The Yes campaign's rebuttal says qualifying spending "CAN INCLUDE" transportation, interpretation, care coordination, outreach, nurse managers, medical equipment and information technology. The No argument says the measure "restricts clinics from funding mammogram, X-ray and CT machines, information technology and expanding or upgrading clinics." The text settles neither claim; it leaves the line to the Attorney General's guidance. The LAO says the outcome of that guidance is one of two things its cost estimate depends on.

Together they reported $3.28 billion in revenue. On the measure's starting numbers, none reaches 90%: their combined ratio is 77.4%, and the gap to 90% totals $412.5 million.

Family Health Centers of San Diego has the lowest ratio, 64.5%, and the largest gap, $124.6 million. The others: WellSpace Health 77.9% ($20.7 million), TrueCare 73.8% ($21.2 million), North East Medical Services 73.5% ($63.5 million), Neighborhood Healthcare 72.0% ($48.7 million) and Innercare 64.7% ($28.6 million).

Proposition 44 sets a 90% "Mission Spend Ratio" for nonprofit community health clinics
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop44-text-proposed-laws.pdf) introduces a single number, the "Mission Spend Ratio": the total a clinic spends on "activities that accomplish each clinic's exempt purpose" divided by its total revenue. A clinic below 90% owes a penalty.

It excludes clinics run by federally recognized tribes, tribal organizations and urban Indian organizations. Public clinics, such as those run by counties, are not covered; the LAO describes the rule as applying to "private nonprofit safety net clinics."
The starting figures come from each clinic's federal tax return. The text says spending on the clinic's purpose "will be based on" the "total program service expenses" on line 4e of Part III of IRS Form 990, and revenue on line 12 of Part I, both "as of calendar year 2024." From there the Attorney General may issue "binding guidance" that adjusts both numbers: counting some spending the 990 does not classify as program services, excluding some that it does, and tightening the reporting of payments to "related parties" such as management companies, landlords and affiliated foundations, so that money routed through them cannot inflate the ratio. The Attorney General must publish findings explaining that guidance and can issue it through bulletins rather than formal regulations.
Each clinic files the data with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers every year. Within 90 days the Attorney General calculates every clinic's ratio, sends it to the clinic and the California Department of Public Health, and posts it online. Clinics pay a new annual fee set to cover the cost of running the program.
The 10% left over must cover administration and any surplus
Because the ratio is measured against revenue rather than spending, the remaining 10% has to absorb two different things: everything the clinic spends outside program services, such as administration, finance, human resources and fundraising, and any money it takes in but does not spend that year. A clinic that runs a surplus to build reserves or save for a new building lowers its ratio by exactly that amount, even if its spending is all on patient care.
That design is deliberate. The measure's findings say some clinics report management and administrative expenses of "30 to 40 percent of total revenue" while others spend under 10%, and that "many clinics are highly profitable, sometimes reporting annual surpluses of as much as 20 percent of total revenue, rather than spending the funds in a manner consistent with their charitable mission." Its stated intent is "a reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed spending as a proportion of total revenue."
What counts as patient care is the contested part. The Yes campaign's rebuttal says qualifying spending "CAN INCLUDE" transportation, interpretation, care coordination, outreach, nurse managers, medical equipment and information technology. The No argument says the measure "restricts clinics from funding mammogram, X-ray and CT machines, information technology and expanding or upgrading clinics." The text settles neither claim; it leaves the line to the Attorney General's guidance. The LAO says the outcome of that guidance is one of two things its cost estimate depends on.

Relief Not applicable One-year waivers for unexpected circumstances or a threat to the clinic’s survival as a going concern
Enforcement Attorney General oversight of charities Any patient may sue for breach of charitable trust; fines of $5,000, then $10,000 a month, for late reports; jail for knowing misreporting

Start date Not applicable Each clinic’s first full fiscal year beginning at least six months after passage
Seven clinics funding the No campaign: Mission Spend Ratios from 64.5% to 83.9%
To show what the ratio looks like in practice, we applied the measure's starting formula to the 2024 Form 990s of seven clinics on the No campaign's list of top contributors at the Fair Political Practices Commission. Together they reported $3.28 billion in revenue. On the measure's starting numbers, none reaches 90%: their combined ratio is 77.4%, and the gap to 90% totals $412.5 million.
AltaMed, the No campaign's largest donor and the largest of the seven at $1.72 billion in revenue, spent $1.44 billion on program services, a ratio of 83.9% and a gap of $105.2 million. Family Health Centers of San Diego has the lowest ratio, 64.5%, and the largest gap, $124.6 million. The others: WellSpace Health 77.9% ($20.7 million), TrueCare 73.8% ($21.2 million), North East Medical Services 73.5% ($63.5 million), Neighborhood Healthcare 72.0% ($48.7 million) and Innercare 64.7% ($28.6 million).
The reasons differ, which is why the revenue breakdown matters. Innercare's management and fundraising expenses equal 29.8% of its revenue, the highest of the seven. WellSpace Health spent 93.5% of its total expenses on program services but ran a surplus equal to 16.6% of revenue, so its ratio falls to 77.9%. Family Health Centers of San Diego (16.3%) and Neighborhood Healthcare (14.4%) also ran double-digit surpluses. AltaMed's surplus was 4.0% of revenue.
Proposition 44's Mission Spend Ratio is falling short of 90% at seven community health clinics funding the No campaign, on their 2024 tax returns before any Attorney General adjustments. These figures come with limits. They are the measure's starting point, before any guidance from the Attorney General, which could raise or lower every ratio. The seven are large clinics that chose to fund the opposition, not a sample of California's health centers. Three report on a July–June fiscal year, so their "2024" return covers July 2024 through June 2025. And a single year's revenue can include capital grants or investment gains that swell the surplus. The statewide reads come from the LAO: an average of about 80% on health care services, and "most FQHCs spend less than 90 percent," in the words of its September 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0008A1%29.pdf) to the Attorney General.
The same filings report executive pay, the Yes campaign's main target. AltaMed's president and chief executive, Castulo de la Rocha, received $1,949,272 in total compensation in 2024, according to the return's Schedule J. North East Medical Services reported $1,950,174 for its president and chief executive, Eddie Chan, $1,054,094 of it retirement and deferred compensation. The chief executives of TrueCare, Neighborhood Healthcare and Innercare reported $667,101 to $729,864.
Proposition 44's penalties: Refundable for five years, then spent on the clinic workforce
A clinic below 90% receives a notice from the Department of Public Health within 30 days of the Attorney General's calculation and must pay a penalty equal to the gap: 90% of its revenue minus what it spent on its mission. It can pay within 30 days or appeal to both agencies and get a hearing.
The money is held in escrow for five years. A clinic gets it back if it reaches 90% and agrees with the department on a plan to spend the refund on mission-directed expenses. Money not reclaimed after five years goes to the Legislature to spend on "clinical worker training, recruitment, and retention." Penalties paid and refunds received are excluded from later ratio calculations so they do not distort them.
The Department of Public Health can grant one-year waivers, renewable, that pause the 90% rule or set a different ratio. A clinic qualifies by showing "unexpected or exceptional circumstances," or by showing that meeting the rule "would raise doubts about the clinic's ability to continue as a going concern," with the department weighing likely closures, lost services and jobs, whether the clinic is small, rural or frontier, and whether a closure would cut access in its region.
Enforcement goes beyond the penalty:
Reporting fines. A clinic that fails to file owes $5,000 for a first violation and $10,000 for each further month.
Patient lawsuits. If a clinic fails to report, or falls below 90% without a waiver, "any patient of that FQHC" can sue to remedy a breach of charitable trust. "Good faith" is not a defense, and the business judgment rule that normally protects nonprofit boards does not apply.
Criminal penalties. A director, officer or agent who knowingly misreports, or routes money through related parties, "with intent to artificially increase their Mission Spend Ratio," faces up to a year in county jail or a term under the state's realignment sentencing law.
The rule starts with each clinic's "first full fiscal year beginning at least 6 months after passage." On our reading of that clause, that is July 1, 2027 for clinics with a July–June fiscal year and January 1, 2028 for calendar-year clinics. The Legislature can amend the law only "to further the purposes of this act."

The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) puts state enforcement costs, reviewing financial reports and investigating clinics, "in the low tens of millions of dollars per year," paid by the fees the measure charges clinics. The larger effects are ones it cannot size. "Some clinics that could not meet the minimum spending requirement might close instead," which would shift costs to public providers. The letter's summary: the net effect "could range from limited to extensive." Our 2026–27 health budget guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/state-budget/2026-27-california-health-budget-guide-medi-cal-updates-cuts-coverages-and-timelines/) covers the Medi-Cal changes already under way.
The LAO uses two counts that look inconsistent and are not. Its ballot analysis refers to "about 2,000 safety net clinics," most private nonprofits and the rest public. The proponents of record are Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming, according to the Attorney General's active-measures list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) (file 25-0008, title and summary issued October 7, 2025). The Yes campaign's contact in the Voter Information Guide is SEIU-UHW, and Brown signs the ballot argument as "Initiative Proponent" alongside a community clinic worker. A bill with a similar aim, AB 1113, titled "Federally qualified health centers: mission spend ratio," died on January 31, 2026, the deadline for that year's two-year bills to pass their house of origin; CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) that the union tried "last year" to pass a bill with nearly the same effect. SEIU-UHW is also the sponsor of Prop 40, the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/).
The two money sources measure different things. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-44-requires-community-health-clinics-spend-90-percent-revenue-program-services-initiative-statute) reports $10.8 million contributed to the Yes committee through October 6, and $21.6 million to the No committee, which is sponsored by California Primary Care Association Advocates, the clinics' trade group. The FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 13, shows $16.9 million to the Yes committee, all of it from SEIU-UHW's political issues committee, but marks the figure with an asterisk. The FPPC uses that mark when a contribution went to a committee formed for more than one ballot measure, where "it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure." On both sources the No side's committee has raised more.
The No committee's ten largest donors gave $17.4 million, almost all of it from clinics. AltaMed leads with $6.1 million, followed by the California Primary Care Association Advocates' issues committee ($2.1 million), Family Health Centers of San Diego ($1.5 million), WellSpace Health and North East Medical Services ($1.5 million each), San Ysidro Health ($1.0 million), TrueCare and Innercare ($1.0 million each), Neighborhood Healthcare ($0.9 million) and the Community Health Center Network/Alameda Health Consortium ($0.8 million).
The fight has also moved to court. The California Primary Care Association and several clinics sued SEIU-UHW in federal court in September, CalMatters reported, alleging that the union offered to drop Prop 44 in exchange for more union membership at clinics or for the association to drop its opposition to the billionaire tax; a union spokesperson called the allegations "categorically false." An earlier association lawsuit seeking to remove the measure from the ballot was dismissed.

The FPPC uses that mark when a contribution went to a committee formed for more than one ballot measure, where "it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure." On both sources the No side's committee has raised more.
The No committee's ten largest donors gave $17.4 million, almost all of it from clinics. AltaMed leads with $6.1 million, followed by the California Primary Care Association Advocates' issues committee ($2.1 million), Family Health Centers of San Diego ($1.5 million), WellSpace Health and North East Medical Services ($1.5 million each), San Ysidro Health ($1.0 million), TrueCare and Innercare ($1.0 million each), Neighborhood Healthcare ($0.9 million) and the Community Health Center Network/Alameda Health Consortium ($0.8 million).

An earlier association lawsuit seeking to remove the measure from the ballot was dismissed.

- Timing: federal Medicaid cuts (HR 1 / One Big Beautiful Bill) expected to cause 2M Californians to lose insurance by 2030, up to $30B in health care funding losses in 2027. Imposing this now is worst-case timing.

**It's a bargaining chip, not reform.** CPCA filed a federal RICO suit alleging Regan offered to pull Prop 44 if CPCA backed unionizing 25,000 workers. The dead legislative version (AB 1113) would have *exempted* clinics that created "labor-management cooperation committees." SEIU-UHW has spent $216M+ on such measures — three dialysis props ($340M, all rejected), most others withdrawn after concessions.

**Consensus:** No from Newsom, both state parties, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the California Chamber, Planned Parenthood, CMA, AAP-CA, AAFP, ACOG, ACEP, school nurses, and 300+ organizations. Every major editorial board — SF Chronicle, LA Times, McClatchy, Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register, and progressive GrowSF — says no. Polling: 25% yes / 71% no, the least popular of 14 measures. Sole funder: SEIU-UHW ($16.9M vs. $38.6M against).

The accountability concern is real, but this instrument fines the safety net for being solvent, leaves its core term undefined, and serves a labor dispute. Fix executive pay with a pay cap; get transparency from already-public 990s.

**No.**

## My research

**What it does:** Prop 44 (SEIU-UHW's "Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act") forces nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers to spend 90% of **total revenue** on "program services," with a penalty equal to the full shortfall, plus a private right of action for any patient, criminal penalties, and the definition of "program services" left to post-election "binding guidance" from the Attorney General.

**The decisive problem — it penalizes solvency, not waste.** Because the denominator is *revenue*, not *expenses*, a clinic that runs a prudent surplus gets fined even if every dollar it spends goes to care. The Legislative Analyst confirms clinics average ~80%. Brad Fulton (Indiana University's Philanthropy Research Hub, **not** involved in the fight), analyzing actual Form 990s for the Sacramento Bee, found **89% of 147 California clinic organizations would fail**, facing $1.6B in first-year fines — and of the 16 that passed, **all but two were operating in the red**. His conclusion: *"Almost no health center in the U.S. meets Prop. 44's standard."* A measure only financially distressed clinics can satisfy is a broken measure. California Today's independent replication shows the same: WellSpace spent 93.5% of *expenses* on program services but scored 77.9% purely because it ran a reserve.

**It doesn't even do what it advertises.** The findings target $1.95M CEO salaries, but the operative text caps nothing — executive pay counts identically to a bookkeeper's salary. And the "transparency" benefit is largely already free: Form 990 data is public on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, which is exactly how these ratios were computed without Prop 44.

**Wrong targets, worst timing.** It hits only the nonprofit safety net (not hospitals, not for-profits) serving 1 in 4 Medi-Cal patients — precisely as federal Medicaid cuts threaten ~2M Californians with coverage loss and up to $30B in state health funding.

**It's a bargaining chip, not reform.** CPCA filed a federal RICO suit alleging Regan offered to pull Prop 44 if CPCA backed unionizing 25,000 workers. The dead legislative version (AB 1113) would have *exempted* clinics that created "labor-management cooperation committees." SEIU-UHW has spent $216M+ on such measures — three dialysis props ($340M, all rejected), most others withdrawn after concessions.

**Consensus:** No from Newsom, both state parties, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the California Chamber, Planned Parenthood, CMA, AAP-CA, AAFP, ACOG, ACEP, school nurses, and 300+ organizations. Every major editorial board — SF Chronicle, LA Times, McClatchy, Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register, and progressive GrowSF — says no. Polling: 25% yes / 71% no, the least popular of 14 measures. Sole funder: SEIU-UHW ($16.9M vs. $38.6M against).

The accountability concern is real, but this instrument fines the safety net for being solvent, leaves its core term undefined, and serves a labor dispute. Fix executive pay with a pay cap; get transparency from already-public 990s.

**No.**

Proposition 44
Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Safety Net Clinics Serve Low-Income People. Clinics are places where people can access certain health care services, such as doctor's visits. Many clinics are considered "safety net," as they mainly serve low-income and uninsured people. The care they provide is often low cost or free to patients. There are about 2,000 safety net clinics in California. Most are private nonprofits, and the rest are run by public entities (such as counties).
Clinics Spend Most of Their Revenue on Health Care Services. Clinics spend most of their revenue on providing health care to patients. They also have other expenses, such as administrative costs. Each year, private nonprofit safety net clinics in California report their revenues and expenses to the federal government and the state. These clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services, though the percent varies across clinics.
Proposal
Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics. Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. This means that spending on other expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue. The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related to providing health care services, and which are other expenses, using existing reports to the federal government as a starting point. Affected clinics could ask the state for a temporary waiver of the requirements in some cases.
Creates Penalty for Falling Short of Minimum. Proposition 44 requires affected clinics to pay a penalty to the state if they fall short of the new health care spending minimum. The penalty would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum. Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years. If clinics do not comply within five years, the state would keep the money and spend it on clinic workforce programs.
Fiscal Effects
Creates State Enforcement Costs. Under Proposition 44, the state would enforce the new requirements on private nonprofit safety net clinics. This includes reviewing financial reports and investigating affected entities. State enforcement costs would be in the low tens of millions of dollars per year. The proposition directs the state to cover the costs by charging fees on affected clinics.
Could Have Other Uncertain Costs. Proposition 44 could create other costs for the state and local governments. These costs are uncertain. They depend on (1) how the state Attorney General would define health care-related expenses and (2) whether affected clinics would meet the spending minimum. For example, affected clinics might spend more on direct health care services to comply with the requirement, which could increase state costs. This is because some of these services would be for patients in Medi-Cal, the state's program that provides health care coverage for low-income Californians. Some clinics that could not meet the minimum spending requirement might close instead. This would create other uncertain effects on state and local costs.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year to enforce the new requirements on certain private nonprofit health care clinics, covered by fees charged to the affected clinics.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute” (circulating title and summary issued by the attorney general, October 7, 2025). The measure’s own name is the “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.”
Type: Initiated state statute (AG No. 25-0008A1). It adds new sections to the Government Code and the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Nonprofit federally qualified health centers must spend at least 90 percent of their total annual revenue on mission-related “program services” or pay a penalty equal to the shortfall. Clinics must report the underlying figures to the attorney general, who publishes a “mission spend ratio” for each clinic.
A vote NO means: No revenue-spending floor is imposed on these clinics. Their spending stays governed by existing nonprofit and federal-grant rules and by their own boards.
Sponsor/proponent: Californians for Responsible Healthcare, sponsored by SEIU-UHW West (Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West). Proponents of record are Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted about 1.03 million signatures on April 1, 2026, against a 546,651 valid signature requirement, and the secretary of state projected enough valid signatures to qualify for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0008A1, “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 2025-008 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-008)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 44 would set a spending floor on California’s nonprofit community health clinics. Each covered clinic would have to spend at least 90 percent of its total annual revenue on “program services” that advance its charitable mission, meaning patient care and related services rather than management, overhead, or accumulated surplus [1, Sec. 3].
The measure works through a ratio it calls the mission spend ratio. That ratio is the amount a clinic spends on activities accomplishing its exempt purpose divided by its total revenue [1, Sec. 3]. The building blocks come from the clinic’s IRS Form 990. The numerator starts from “total program service expenses” on line 4e of Part III, and the denominator starts from total revenue on line 12 of Part I, for tax year 2024 or later [1, Sec. 3(b)(1)]. The attorney general may issue binding guidance adjusting how both figures are counted, so the final definition of qualifying spending is not fixed in the text—it is delegated [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
A clinic whose mission spend ratio falls below 90 percent would owe an administrative penalty equal to the gap between what it actually spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of its total revenue [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)]. Penalty money is held in escrow in a state fund for five years. A clinic can get the money back if it comes into compliance and agrees with the Department of Public Health on a plan to spend the returned funds on mission-directed expenses. Money not returned within five years is appropriated for clinic-worker training, recruitment, and retention [1, Sec. 4(a)]. The Department of Public Health can grant one-year waivers for unexpected or exceptional circumstances or where compliance would raise going-concern doubts under generally accepted accounting principles [1, Sec. 4(c)]. Separate reporting fines of $5,000 for a first violation and $10,000 per month thereafter apply to clinics that do not file on time [1, Sec. 3(d)].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0008A1, “Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act” (as amended September 2025), California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
Key language:
“‘Mission Spend Ratio’ is the total amount spent on activities that accomplish each clinic’s exempt purpose divided by that clinic’s total revenue.” [1, Sec. 3(a)(2)]
“The Department of Public Health shall annually assess on each clinic subject to Section 12586.3 of the Government Code that has a Mission Spend Ratio below ninety percent (90%) an administrative penalty equal to the difference between the amount the clinic spent on mission-directed expenses and 90 percent of the clinic’s total revenue.” [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)]
What it amends: Adds Section 12586.3 to the Government Code (reporting and the mission spend ratio) and Section 1234.1 to the Health and Safety Code (penalties and the escrow fund) [1, Secs. 3-4]. As an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it only in ways consistent with the measure’s terms.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? The covered universe is narrow. A “clinic” under the measure means a nonprofit clinic corporation that is a federally qualified health center (FQHC) under federal law, and it expressly includes “FQHC Look-Alikes,” which meet FQHC program requirements without receiving the federal grant [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)]. The measure excludes federally recognized tribes, tribal organizations, and urban Indian organizations [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)]. It does not reach hospitals, for-profit clinics, or medical groups. The sponsor is SEIU-UHW West, a union representing roughly 120,000 healthcare workers, through the committee Californians for Responsible Healthcare. The opposition is led by the California Primary Care Association and allied clinics, operating as Protect Patients California.
What? A hard floor requiring at least 90 percent of total revenue to go to program services, enforced by a penalty equal to the shortfall, plus annual reporting and a state-published mission spend ratio for every covered clinic [1, Secs. 3-4].
Where? Statewide, applied to every nonprofit FQHC and FQHC Look-Alike operating in California.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The mission spend ratio calculation is built on Form 990 data for tax year 2024 or later, and the attorney general must make each clinic’s data public within ninety days of receipt [1, Sec. 3(b)(4)].
Why? The proponents’ findings say many clinics spend excessive shares of revenue on executive compensation and administration, that some report surpluses as high as 20 percent of revenue, and that clinic workers face chronic understaffing and turnover. The stated intent is to create “a reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed spending” so that patient care and workforce stability are prioritized over management and overhead [1, Sec. 2].
4. Trade-offs
Proposition 44 is one front in a long-running fight between SEIU-UHW and the California healthcare industry. The union placed three measures in this cycle: this clinic-spending floor, an executive-pay cap on hospitals and medical groups, and a billionaire wealth tax. The hospital industry answered with its own initiative requiring unions to get member approval before large political spending. Union-backed healthcare measures in California have a track record of functioning as leverage in labor-management disputes, most visibly the dialysis fights of 2018 through 2020, where roughly $340 million was spent and every measure failed. Reading Proposition 44 only as a patient-care reform, and not also as a bargaining instrument, misses half of what it is.
That does not make the underlying concern fake. FQHCs are nonprofit, tax-exempt, and heavily taxpayer funded. There is no serious dispute that some accumulate large surpluses or pay executives generously while frontline staffing lags. Requiring that a defined, high share of revenue flows to program services, while publishing each clinic’s ratio, is a coherent accountability idea with real appeal. The patient-care-first framing is not a pretext for nothing.
The hard question is whether a rigid revenue ratio is the right tool. Three features cut against it. First, the denominator is total revenue, not expenses. A clinic that runs a prudent operating surplus or builds reserves for a lean year is mechanically pushed below 90 percent and penalized, even if every dollar it spends is spent well. The measure effectively caps nonprogram spending plus surplus plus reserves at a combined 10 percent of revenue. Second, “program services” is anchored to a single Form 990 line, and the opposition argues that essential functions such as interpretation, transportation, and case management may not count, so clinics could be penalized for spending that patients experience as care. Third, the definition is not actually fixed. The attorney general may issue binding guidance moving the line in either direction, which concentrates significant discretion over clinic finances in one elected office [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
The measure tries to soften the edges with waivers for going-concern risk and for rural or distressed clinics, with a five-year window to earn penalties back [1, Sec. 4]. Whether those valves are wide enough is the crux. An opposition analysis commissioned by the clinics estimated that more than 90 percent of clinic organizations would face penalties totaling about $1.7 billion in the first year. That figure comes from an interested party and should be treated as a claim, not a finding, but even a fraction of it would fall on the safety-net providers that serve California’s lowest-income patients at the same moment federal Medicaid reductions are tightening their budgets.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Proposition 44 creates a clear, published accountability metric for nonprofit clinics that receive large amounts of public money, letting the state and the public see how much of each clinic’s revenue reaches program services [1, Sec. 3(b)(4)].
It targets a real pattern the proponents document, in which some clinics report administrative costs of 30 to 40 percent of revenue or surpluses near 20 percent while frontline staffing suffers [1, Sec. 2].
Recovered penalties are steered toward clinic-worker training, recruitment, and retention, which addresses the understaffing the findings describe [1, Sec. 4(a)].
The escrow-and-refund design means a clinic that corrects course can recover its penalty rather than simply losing the money [1, Sec. 4(a)].
Waiver provisions for going-concern risk and for small, rural, or frontier clinics give the Department of Public Health room to protect the most vulnerable providers [1, Sec. 4(c)].
Potential risks
The floor is measured against total revenue, so a clinic can be penalized for running a prudent surplus or building reserves even when its actual spending is sound [1, Sec. 4(b)(1)].
Anchoring “program services” to one Form 990 line may exclude services patients rely on, such as interpretation, transportation, and case management, penalizing spending that functions as care.
The measure hands the attorney general broad discretion to redefine the numerator and denominator through binding guidance, concentrating power over clinic finances in an elected partisan office [1, Sec. 3(b)(2)].
It applies only to nonprofit FQHCs and Look-Alikes, the core of the safety net, and not to hospitals or for-profit providers, so the burden lands on the clinics serving the lowest-income patients [1, Sec. 3(a)(1)].
Penalties could reach from the hundreds of millions to more than a billion dollars in the first year on the opposition’s estimate, arriving alongside federal Medicaid cuts that are already straining clinic budgets.
The California Primary Care Association has a pending federal lawsuit arguing the measure conflicts with federal law governing FQHCs, so passage may not settle whether it can take effect.
The Legislative Analyst estimates state enforcement costs in the low tens of millions of dollars annually, partly offset by fees and penalties on the clinics themselves.
6. Open questions
How will the attorney general define “program services,” and will functions such as interpretation, transportation, and case management count toward the 90 percent?
Because the floor is measured against revenue, how will clinics that need operating surpluses or reserves avoid penalties without cutting into their financial cushion?
How many of California’s roughly 1,300-plus FQHC sites would actually fall below 90 percent under the final definition, and what is the realistic total penalty exposure once waivers are applied?
Will the Department of Public Health’s waiver process move fast enough to keep a distressed or rural clinic open before a penalty forces service cuts?
Does the measure conflict with federal FQHC funding and reimbursement rules, and how will the pending federal lawsuit resolve that before it can take effect?
Is a ballot-locked revenue ratio the right instrument for a problem that varies clinic by clinic, or would board-level and grant-level oversight fit better?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
“Spend 90 percent on patient care” sounds like a floor no one could oppose. But the measure counts spending against total revenue, ties “care” to one tax-form line the attorney general can redefine, and applies only to the nonprofit clinics that serve California’s poorest patients. Before you vote, ask whether this rewards clinics that spend well or mainly penalizes clinics that keep a surplus.
This measure sits inside a labor-industry fight, sponsored and fully funded by one union that has three measures on this ballot. Ask whether Proposition 44 would mostly change how safety-net clinics deliver care, or how much leverage one side carries into its next dispute with the healthcare industry.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.
